title: (R35) Decide how two machines' index rows reach the store repository
description:
Open decision for the user, raised 2026-09-22 after choosing one campaign per machine.

Both machines commit to the same store repository, but today only the top-level index.tsv is committed and campaign indexes stay local. Two writers appending rows to one committed TSV will conflict on most pushes.

Two ways out. Preferred: commit each campaign's index under its own path and derive the top-level index.tsv with a small tool, so it is generated and never hand-merged. This reverses the rule in CLAUDE.md that keeps campaigns out of git. Cheaper but fragile: keep one file, mark it merge=union in .gitattributes, and put the machine name in every test id; one re-sort of the file then silently duplicates rows.

Either way, beads syncs through the Dolt ref on the shared remote, so both machines pull before every push and nothing else is needed for the tracker. Findings and the run log take dated entries appended at the end only.
close_reason: Decided by the user 2026-09-22: campaign records go to the same private store, one directory per campaign, and the store now commits each campaign's text files and the report PDFs (store commit of 2026-09-22). Bundles and runner logs stay local. A campaign belongs to one machine, so no two machines write the same file.

title: Next rung: the timestep controller gains on rung 1, if the user sends them up
description:
The screening found one lead: kI=0.3, kP=0.7 with lag 1 is 0.46 of lag 1 alone on test4_3.0-3.2ms (72, 73, 72 s, deterministic) and 1.41 on test4_4.0-4.1ms. title: Did the cheapest lag-1 full run resolve the transient? Correctness check at 2-6 ms
description:
The cheapest lag-1 rung-2 repeat (test4_0.0-100.0ms-2026-09-22-4f121db8-3) crossed the 2-4 ms output interval in 4.8k RHS evaluations against the baseline's 701k, which is the "coasted" signature the run skill warns about. Its final Ne matches the other repeats to 4e-5, but the campaign's [correctness] section is never read by the runner and the extractor writes no_reference, so nobody has checked whether the transient itself was resolved.

Do: compare the three lag-1 repeats and one baseline against the parent test4_0.0-100.0ms-2026-09-19-neutlag-va over 2-6 ms on the campaign's own quantities, ne_target_max and te_target_max, at every output, with the postprocess skill. If the cheap path skipped the transient the rung-2 win is 0.72, not 0.38-0.55, and the finding must be corrected. The dumps of the four rung-2 cases must survive pruning until this is done: keep_recent is 20 and the campaign is idle, so they are safe for now.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22 morning with a scratchpad script (correctness.py) that opens the parent and the six rung-2 runs with xhermes and calls the extractor's own _physics_series, so the quantities are the index's ne_target_max and te_target_max. Against the parent at matching output times: the three baselines deviate at most 0.7 per cent over 0-10 ms; the three lag-1 runs at most 2.8 per cent in ne and 2.3 per cent in te, the worst output being 2 ms, and the cheapest repeat (r3) is no worse than the other two. Endpoints at 100 ms agree to under 0.05 per cent. All six pass the campaign's window tolerance of 0.20 and endpoint tolerance of 0.05. Traces saved in campaigns/test4-jacobian/rung2_traces.csv. Caveat: the check sees the 2 ms output grid only, so a sub-interval excursion between outputs would not show; the runner should still gain an automated check (so-37r).

title: Solver path is not deterministic through the 2-6 ms transient, and lag 1 amplifies it
description:
Three rung-2 lag-1 repeats (test4_0.0-100.0ms-2026-09-22-4f121db8, -2, -3) started from a seed identical to eleven digits in Ne, with byte-identical BOUT.inp, and did 4455, 3104 and 2442 nonlinear iterations, at an identical 0.45 s per iteration. The whole difference is in the 2-6 ms transient: 351k, 90k and 4.8k RHS evaluations in the 2-4 ms output interval against the baseline's 701k. Before 2 ms and after 6 ms the runs agree to a few per cent, and the final Ne agrees to 4e-5. The baseline (lag 3) shows the same effect at 6 per cent in nl_its. See findings.md, "Repeat spread is the solver's path".

Open question: what is the source of the non-determinism (MPI reduction order, MUMPS pivoting, the PID timestep controller reacting to a rejected step) and why lag 1 amplifies it. A first step is to diff the timestep history of the three runs from BOUT.log.0 and find the first step where they part. Until it is understood, three repeats give a range not a mean for any window containing 2-6 ms.
notes:
Study 3 adds the noise rung: test4_2.0-3.0ms moves off rung 0 and every cell on
it runs ten times. The bare baseline, lag 1 and the controller gains are three
of those cells, so the night ends with ten draws of each on the window that
holds the 2.65 ms cliff, against the three draws this issue was opened on. Five
failure-handling settings and three controller-gain points get ten draws there
too, which says whether any of them changes how often the cheap path happens.
2026-09-23: store investigation I02 (repeat-divergence) compared the step logs of all 870 repeat runs. Seeds are byte-identical. MUMPS and SuperLU_DIST repeats part at round-off within a median 11 steps; ASM, block Jacobi and STRUMPACK repeats stay bit-identical. The right-hand side is deterministic. Cost spread builds in 2.5-6 ms: each repeat crosses cheaply or spends over 1000 Newton iterations. Next, needs a run: one-process MUMPS repeats, or STRUMPACK repeats on the full run.
2026-09-23 correction: only the gains come close to two outcomes in 2.5-6 ms (64-328 against about 1370 iterations); lag 1 and the baseline all enter the costly phase and spread without a gap. Report: store investigations/I02-2026-09-23-repeat-divergence, page https://claude.ai/artifact/AcWfu1BM5hyMwjzHYJ8nZn

title: (R17) check_overrides ignores the search space's depends field
description:
search-space.toml declares a depends field on 65 knobs, and check_overrides in perftest/runner.py validates only the knob's name, its choice membership, its switch spelling and its numeric range. It never reads depends. A study can therefore queue a configuration the search space already knows cannot apply, and the machine time is spent before anything notices.

Two concrete cases from the 2026-09-21 overnight plan: petsc:pc_factor_mat_solver_type carries depends = {solver:pc_type = lu} and would have been set alongside bjacobi, asm and gamg, where PETSc never consumes it and the extractor then refuses the whole extraction; and solver:pc_type = ilu on 10 ranks, which PETSc cannot build because its ILU is sequential.

Enforcing depends in check_overrides would have caught six of nine screening runs before launch.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: check_overrides resolves each knob's depends against the override, else the recipe's setting, else the search space's `current`; refuses with the condition named; "not x", "a or b" and boolean forms handled; a knob nothing sets leaves the condition unknown, not refused. load_study takes recipes_dir and run_campaign passes it. Tests cover the four cases.

title: (R17) A killed run costs the slot-hour budget nothing
description:
A run the runner kills records outcome=timeout with wall_s blank, because wall_s is read from the log's finish stamp which a killed run never writes. slot_hours_spent sums wall_s, so a killed run costs the budget nothing. A slot can therefore burn hours on killed runs while the 30 slot-hour gate never moves. Confirmed on four rows of the test4-jacobian index (two timeout, two crashed, all wall_s blank).

Fix: charge the budget the elapsed time of the attempt. extract.py already derives an elapsed time from the dump series for classification but does not write it.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: new index column elapsed_s, the seconds an attempt held its slot (log finish stamp, else the dump's last wall_time), written for killed runs too; slot_hours_spent sums elapsed_s and falls back to wall_s. schema.md documents it. Test covers it.

title: (R17) Long windows stall-kill because NOUT is fixed at 50
description:
make_window.py hard-codes NOUT = 50, so a 0-100 ms window writes an output every 2 ms while the parent wrote every 1 ms. The parent spent 1360 s on 3-4 ms and 226 s on 2-3 ms, so one 2 ms output interval is about 1590 s at concurrency 2.0, against a stall_s of 1800 s. The baseline has a 12 per cent margin and any configuration slower than baseline is stall-killed mid-run. Found by an adversarial review of the 2026-09-21 overnight plan; confirmed at hermes-perftest/make_window.py:35 and campaign.toml stall_s.

Options: raise stall_s for long windows, scale NOUT with window length so the cadence matches the parent, or define the long rung as 0-50 ms where 50 outputs land every 1 ms. The test costs 1-4 s per ms after 6 ms, so 50-100 ms adds under 200 s and a 0-50 ms window holds nearly all the cost.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: make_window.py gains --nout (submodule, on the window-scheme branch, commit pending the user's say), and the runner passes at least one output per millisecond (outputs_for: max(50, ceil(length_ms))). design.md step 4 updated. Test covers the count.

title: The kill cutoff ratchets to the fastest run and erases the slow half of the curve
description:
The runner kills a run at cutoff_factor times the best time recorded for its window. The best is the fastest run ever seen, so one unusually fast configuration ratchets the cutoff down for every configuration after it, including the baseline.

Seen 2026-09-21 on test4_2.0-3.0ms in the test4-jacobian campaign. The cutoff moved 360 min (no completed run) -> 11 min (3x the baseline's 213 s) -> 2 min (3x lag_jacobian=1's 36 s). The next configuration, lag_jacobian=10, was killed at 2 min and recorded as a timeout. The baseline for that same window takes 213 s, so under the ratcheted cutoff the baseline itself would now be killed.

Why this matters beyond one row. The campaign exists to find the shape of a knob's cost curve. Killing everything slower than the fastest point erases the slow half of that curve, and a timeout carries no usable time, so nothing can be plotted against it. Worse, the faster the winner, the more of the curve is destroyed - the flaw bites hardest exactly when the campaign is succeeding.

It also makes a long unattended study unsafe. Overnight, one fast configuration early on would turn most later runs into timeouts and waste the night.

Options. Anchor the cutoff to the BASELINE's time for that window rather than the best, since the baseline is the reference every result is read against and is known before the study starts. Or take the median of recorded times rather than the minimum. Or keep a floor under the cutoff so it can never fall below the baseline. The first is simplest to explain and matches what cutoff_factor is meant to express: how much worse than the reference is worth waiting for.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-09-21. cutoff_s now anchors on baseline_wall, the fastest completed run of that window at the campaign's own recipe with nothing varied, and falls back to best_wall only while no baseline exists. best_wall stays, as the campaign's best time, but no longer sets the kill time.

Checked against the live test4-jacobian index: test4_2.0-3.0ms moves from a 2 min cutoff, which had killed lag_jacobian=10 and 20, to 10.7 min, anchored on the baseline's 213 s.

Four tests hold it: a fast variant does not shorten the cutoff and the baseline survives its own cutoff; the best anchors it until a baseline exists; a row of another recipe with nothing varied does not anchor it. 157 tests pass.

Still open and NOT fixed here: the two killed rows in the campaign are timeouts with no usable time, so the lag 10 and lag 20 points on test4_2.0-3.0ms have to be re-run to complete that curve.

title: Disk budget is set so pruning never fires, and an overnight campaign dies on the floor
description:
The runner prunes dumps only when a campaign's recorded dumps exceed [disk] budget_gb. The example and the test4-jacobian campaign both set that to 200 GB. The filesystem has 92 GB free and [disk] floor_gb is 50, so the runner refuses to launch at 42 GB used and the prune never fires once. An unattended campaign therefore stops on the floor instead of reclaiming space.

Measured 2026-09-21: one test4 window case is 278 MB, of which 263 MB is dumps, so pruning recovers 95 per cent of it. 42 GB of headroom is about 150 runs. A 12-hour overnight campaign on three slots at 200 s a run is about 650 runs, or 180 GB, so it cannot finish without pruning.

can_delete.py is not the obstacle: run against a finished window case it prints "SAFE: an ordinary run whose record is validated" and exits 0.

Fix: budget_gb must be smaller than the free space minus floor_gb, not a number chosen independently of the disk. About 15 GB suits this machine, and keep_recent = 20 at 263 MB needs only 5.3 GB, so the budget is satisfiable.

Better fix: have load_campaign reject a campaign whose budget_gb exceeds the free space on the data directory minus floor_gb. The failure is then a message naming the setting, before anything runs, rather than a campaign that dies hours in.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-09-21. Runner.require_reachable_disk_budget runs once at the top of run(), beside require_approval, and stops the campaign when budget_gb does not fit in the free space above floor_gb. The message names the setting.

The fix is NOT the one this issue proposed. load_campaign already requires floor_gb < budget_gb, and combining that with "budget_gb must fit above the floor" made every budget invalid on this machine: 50 < budget <= 42 has no solution. So the existing rule stands untouched and the settings were made feasible instead. test4-jacobian now runs floor_gb 30, budget_gb 40 against 87 GB free, leaving 57 GB of headroom, and campaign.example.toml ships the same pair with both rules spelled out.

Two tests hold it: an unreachable budget stops, and it stops before any trial is generated. The test fixture now pins free_gb at 500 so no test depends on what this machine has free today.

title: (R35) Two sdtools tools are PATH lookups a fresh VM cannot satisfy
description:
R35 says everything must run under another vendor's agents on a fresh VM. Two tools stop that today.

perftest/runner.py resolves the tools that ship in this repository against TOOL_ROOT, deliberately and with a comment saying why. But two tools stay PATH lookups because they belong to sdtools: APPLY_RECIPE = "apply_recipe.py", and sdrun.py, which is named in the campaign's [machine] launch line.

sdtools is deliberately not being packaged (decided 2026-09-20), so on a fresh VM neither tool is on PATH and there is no pip install that puts them there. The runner gets as far as applying the recipe and dies.

Found 2026-09-21: the same thing nearly happened on THIS machine. The three run screens date from 2026-08-31, before the shell lines that add the two cli directories to PATH, so their PATH has neither sdtools/cli nor this repository's cli, and carries neither the store nor the data variable. The runplan line for the test4-jacobian campaign has to set all three itself.

Two ways out. Either name both tools in the campaign config so a VM can point at wherever sdtools was cloned, which keeps the config path-free by making the path an input; or document a required PATH setup step in the VM instructions and accept that the runner cannot start without it. The first is better because it fails with a message naming the setting.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: runner.resolve_tool() finds a bare tool on PATH, then under $sdtools/cli, and fails naming the variable. Applied to apply_recipe.py and to the launch line's first word. Also: [machine] cores gives one core set per slot and {cores} fills it into the launch line, so a machine without the sdtools launcher pins runs with taskset and mpirun itself. Tests cover both.

title: campaign.example.toml's parent field shows a test_id, but the runner wants a case directory
description:
The [campaign] parent field in campaign.example.toml is set to a test_id (test2_0.0-100.0ms-20260919-201426), and its own comment calls it "a case directory name under <data>/cases". The runner takes the second reading: runner.py line 335 does parent_dir = os.path.join(cases_dir, campaign.parent). So the example as written points at a directory that does not exist, and a campaign copied from it fails when make_window.py is handed a missing parent.

Found 2026-09-21 while writing the test4-jacobian campaign, which uses the case directory name and validates.

Fix: put a case directory name in the example, e.g. test2_0.0-100.0ms-2026-09-19-neutlag-va, and keep the comment. Consider having load_campaign check the parent directory exists, so the failure names the field instead of surfacing inside make_window.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: the example's parent is now the case directory name test2_0.0-100.0ms-2026-09-19-neutlag-va.

title: Gate a run on PETSc's options_left, so a knob that did nothing cannot be recorded as a result
description:
The captured PETSc view for test2_20.0-21.0ms-20260920-160050 begins:

    options_left: ['-d', '-snes_fd_color_use_mat']

PETSc is reporting that it never consumed -snes_fd_color_use_mat. The option sat in the [petsc] section of every run using SNES-MUMPS-3 and did nothing, which is the open puzzle filed as the snes_fd_color_use_mat question.

Every petsc-side knob carries this risk. An option reaches PETSc's database whatever it is named, and it takes effect only if some object calls SetFromOptions and queries it. A campaign can therefore vary a knob through 20 runs, record 20 rows, and have measured one configuration.

PETSc already answers this for free. Ask for options_left, record it as a column, and refuse to record a run whose proposed knob appears in it. That converts a silent null result into a loud one, and it costs nothing per run.

Worth checking at the same time whether options_left is available without the full -snes_view, which is too big to leave on for a long run.
acceptance_criteria: A run whose varied knob appears in PETSc's options_left is not recorded as a result. The column exists in the index and is filled from the run itself.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-21. options_left is an index column, filled from the run's own console log, and the extractor refuses the extraction when a knob the run varied appears in it: that run measured the baseline under another name, so it is kept for inspection and recorded as nothing. An ignored option nobody varied stays a warning, which is what snes_fd_color_use_mat has always been. The recipes that build a PETSc object now set options_left, stating the intent that capture-set.md asked for; those edits are in the hermes-perftest submodule and wait for the user to commit them. CVODE-1 and CVODE-2 are excluded on purpose: they build no PETSc object, and BOUT++ errors on an option nothing read, so a [petsc] section there would stop the run.

title: A [petsc] setting silently overrides the [solver] knob the optimiser moved
description:
BOUT++ applies the [solver] settings with explicit calls and then reads the [petsc] section last: snes.cxx calls SNESSetSolverType, SNESSetTolerances, KSPSetType, PCSetType and the rest, and only at line 770 calls lib.setOptionsFromInputFile(snes), which is SNESSetFromOptions. SNESSetFromOptions descends into the KSP and the PC, so an option in [petsc] overrides the matching [solver] one.

The baseline recipe SNES-MUMPS-3 pins three settings in [petsc] that are also knobs in the search space on the solver side: ksp_type = fgmres, pc_type = lu, snes_linesearch_type = basic.

_set_option in perftest/runner.py edits only the section it is given. So an override of solver:pc_type = ilu leaves [petsc] pc_type = lu in the file. PETSc would run lu; the index row would say ilu. The run is mislabelled, and a mislabelled row is worse than a missing one because it is used.

The same holds for solver:ksp_type against [petsc] ksp_type, and for solver:line_search_type against [petsc] snes_linesearch_type. The line-search case is half-noticed already: the search space entry says "Set only one of the two spellings, or they will disagree", but nothing enforces it and petsc:snes_linesearch_type is not itself a knob, so a proposer cannot set the spelling that wins.

The precedence above is read from the BOUT++ source and from what SNESSetFromOptions does, not measured. One 0.2 ms window with solver:pc_type = ilu against the unchanged recipe would settle it, and the captured -snes_view would say which PC was built.

Options for the fix, for the user to choose: refuse an override whose option also appears in the other managed section; or write the override into both sections; or strip the duplicated settings out of the recipes so each setting has one home.
acceptance_criteria: A campaign cannot produce a row whose recipe says one thing and whose PETSc objects are another. Either the runner refuses the proposal, or it sets both spellings, or the recipes no longer duplicate the setting.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-09-21. perftest/recipe.py now holds the pairs table for the same setting under its two spellings, and the runner refuses an override the recipe would shadow before anything is generated. The recipes no longer write one setting on both sides, and a test holds that against every recipe a campaign may name. The pairs apply to the SNES path only: under type = petsc, BOUT++ spends solver:atol on TSSetTolerances and leaves the SNES tolerance to PETSc, so there the two names really are two settings. The precedence itself is still read from the source rather than measured; the clean test drive is where that gets confirmed from a captured view.

title: The runner cannot find the tools that ship beside it
description:
Found by the first real test drive, 2026-09-20. The runs worked; extraction did not.

The runner calls extract_test.py and can_delete.py by bare name, expecting PATH to supply them. In screen h2 it fails: "test2_0.0-0.2ms: ERROR [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'extract_test.py'". All four runs completed and none was extracted, so four rows sat open as planned with no result.

Cause: the three run screens were created on 31 August, and their PATH predates the .bashrc line that adds hermes-solver-opt/cli. They carry sdtools/cli, which is why apply_recipe.py worked and these two did not. Recreating the screens would fix it until the next time they are old.

The real fix is the one already applied to the window generator: both tools ship in this repository, so resolve them against TOOL_ROOT the way MAKE_WINDOW and DEFAULT_RECIPES are. That stores no path to any machine, because it is relative to the module. apply_recipe.py is different and should stay a PATH lookup: it belongs to sdtools, not here.

Note for whoever does it: the runner carried on to the next trial after the error rather than stopping, which is right, but it means a whole campaign can finish with every row unextracted. Consider whether a failure to run a tool at all, as opposed to a tool that ran and refused, should stop the loop.

Worked around for the test drive by putting the directory on PATH in the runplan line, which is not a fix.
acceptance_criteria: extract_test.py and can_delete.py are resolved against TOOL_ROOT, not PATH. A campaign runs end to end in a screen whose PATH lacks hermes-solver-opt/cli, and every row ends up extracted.
notes:
Done 2026-09-20 in ec3878b: EXTRACT and CAN_DELETE resolve against TOOL_ROOT, run_tool turns an OSError into Stop, and the end-of-campaign line counts every trial. Four tests added, three of which fail against the previous runner.

Not done, and it is the rest of this issue's acceptance criterion: both tools carry `#!/usr/bin/env python3`, so an old screen still runs them under the pyenv shim, whose python has no pandas. Finding the file is fixed; choosing the interpreter is not. Checked: `env PATH=~/.pyenv/shims:/usr/bin:/bin python3 -c "import pandas"` fails with ModuleNotFoundError, and perftest/logparse.py imports pandas at module level, so a real extraction dies there even though --help works.
close_reason: Fixed in two commits on 2026-09-20. The tools resolve against TOOL_ROOT, and they now start under the interpreter that is running the runner rather than under whatever python the shell offers, which was the other half of the same failure. A tool that cannot start at all raises Stop, so the loop ends with the budget unspent instead of producing a campaign of unextracted rows, and the closing line counts every trial. Six tests, five of which fail against the previous runner. Checked against a PATH holding only the pyenv shims and /usr/bin. The clean drive with no PATH workaround in the runplan line belongs to the test-drive issue, which stays open for it.

title: The runner launches in a way this workstation blocks
description:
Raised by the agent that wrote the runner, and not resolved.

campaign.toml's [machine] launch calls the launcher directly, following design.md's rule that the screen and run-plan convention stays out of the tool. This workstation's pre-tool hook blocks exactly that call, because the run-case skill owns launching and requires a slot, a screen and a runplan line.

So the runner as written cannot launch on this machine. Three ways out: the campaign's launch command becomes whatever the run-case skill permits; the runner is driven from inside a screen so its launch is the skill's launch; or the runner writes a runplan line and stops, leaving the launch to a person.

This blocks the end-to-end test drive of a tiny campaign, so it needs settling before the hackathon uses the runner for anything real.
close_reason: Ruled by the user: the run-case skill now admits a driver. Step 5 gains two lines saying a driver that launches its own runs takes one runplan line for the driver, with a comment naming where the driver records the runs it starts, so runstat.py can still find them. The runner already obeyed every other launch rule: the sanctioned launcher, the slot flag, the no-prompt flag, inside a screen. Scored 7/7 against the instruction checklist after a first draft failed on the trigger, the line count and a contradiction with step 5. Committed in agent-instructions and installed.

title: The runner's kill outcome never reaches the index
description:
Found by reading the seam between the two pieces written in parallel on 2026-09-20.

In Runner.run_trial the order is: launch, then extract, then update_row(outcome=KILL_OUTCOME[kill_reason]). The extractor now fills outcome for every run it can classify, and update_row writes blank cells only, with state the single exception. So the runner's write is silently dropped.

What it costs: a run the runner deliberately killed has no finish stamp and no error message in its log, which classify_outcome reads as crashed. A deliberate stop is then recorded as a death. Scoring is unaffected, because best_wall counts only completed rows, so neither crashed nor timeout can move the cutoff. The damage is to the record.

Two ways out, and this needs a ruling rather than a coin toss.

1. The runner stops the run in a way the log records: the BOUT stop file, or the clean-exit signal. classify_outcome then decides from evidence and stays the single decision point, and KILL_OUTCOME is deleted. A cutoff kill still classifies as timeout, because elapsed >= cutoff_s is tested before the cancelled rule. Cost: a genuinely hung run never reads its stop file, so a hard kill has to stay as the fallback, and that case still lands as crashed.

2. update_row overwrites outcome deliberately, as it already does for state, on the grounds that the runner knows something the log cannot: that a person or a budget stopped the run. Cost: two places now decide an outcome.

Option 1 is the better principle and option 2 is the smaller change. Neither is started.
close_reason: Fixed by narrowing the blank-cells-only rule rather than changing how the runner stops a run. update_row takes an overwrite list naming the columns one call may replace, and only the kill branch names outcome; a run that died on its own keeps whatever the extractor read from the log. Verified by breaking the fix and watching the tests fail: the kill test asserted timeout and got completed. 138 tests pass. The test that should have caught this originally stubbed extraction out, so the cell was blank and the correction had nothing to overwrite; it now writes the outcome a real extraction would.

title: Parent dumps must survive until their seeds are cut
description:
The test5 parent's dumps were deleted on 2026-09-20 at 15:25, four minutes after its record was committed to the store at 15:21. title: Jacobian pruning is untried and attacks the 84 percent colouring share
description:
Jacobian pruning is untried and points straight at the 84 percent. It is the
only lever left on Jacobian construction after tightening tolerance, matrix-free
and lag-the-assembled-Jacobian all closed (so-erp).

Mechanism. `prune_jacobian` (snes.cxx:124) scans the assembled Jacobian after
every rebuild, and if more than `prune_fraction` of entries fall below
`prune_abstol` it calls `MatFilter`, compacts the nonzero pattern, and RECOMPUTES
THE COLOURING. The colour count is exactly the number of residual evaluations per
Jacobian build - about 160 on test5. Cutting it cuts the 84 percent directly and
proportionally.

Why there should be anything to cut. BOUT++ builds the sparsity pattern "via
stencil assumptions" (include/bout/petsc_preconditioner.hxx:5, :39) - every
evolved variable assumed to couple to every evolved variable at every stencil
cell. That is a conservative superset, not the true sparsity. Spatially there is
nothing to prune; the prunable part is the all-to-all block in the FIELD
dimension, where most pairs have no direct coupling (impurity density does not
enter main ion momentum except through sources). Colours are roughly stencil
footprint times number of fields, consistent with 160.

Never tried. `prune_jacobian` defaults false and appears in no recipe, no run
record and no finding.

Two regimes, and only the first is free.

(a) prune_abstol = 1e-16, the default. Against normalised values of order one
that is machine epsilon, so it removes only entries the pattern allocated and the
physics never writes. The Jacobian is unchanged as a mathematical object and the
only effect is a cheaper colouring. If the pattern is as conservative as the
header says, this is a pure speedup at zero convergence cost.

(b) prune_abstol raised. Now real couplings go, and it becomes colour count
against failure count - the same cascade that already dominates, since a failure
resets the Jacobian lag (snes.cxx:857).

TRAP, and the reason this is not just a setting to flip. The restore path
(snes.cxx:860) requires `4 * lin_its > 3 * maxl` - Krylov iterations near the cap,
signalling a bad preconditioner. In this configuration `lin_its` EQUALS `nl_its`,
one Krylov iteration per Newton iteration, because matrix_free_operator=false
makes the assembled matrix the operator and MUMPS factorises it exactly (so-8b8).
That condition can never be true here, so an over-pruned Jacobian is never
restored. Worse, pruning the operator does not slow the Krylov solve at all - LU
stays exact for the pruned matrix - it silently returns an inexact Newton step.
The damage appears only as line-search failures, which is precisely the failure
mode already dominating test5 (79 percent LINE_SEARCH, so-erp). Any regime (b)
work needs a guard watching Newton convergence and failure rate, not Krylov
saturation.

Second hazard for regime (b): MatFilter compacts the pattern, so a pruned entry
is invisible until a full restore. A coupling that is negligible while attached
and essential after detachment would be silently absent. Hermes-3 is full of
state-dependent branches - slope limiters, upwind direction, floors, softFloor,
reactions that vanish at a density floor - so "zero at this iterate" and
"structurally zero" are different sets.

First move is cheap and decides whether the rest is worth doing: one short test5
segment, prune_jacobian=true at the 1e-16 default with diagnose on. The code
prints "Pruning Jacobian elements: X / Y" (snes.cxx:155). That ratio is how much
of the assumed pattern is structurally empty. Then compare colour count and
wall-clock against the same segment unpruned.

Also relevant to the hackathon pitch: regime (b) is a search problem under a
34-hour objective with an unguarded failure mode, which is the shape worth taking
to an external collaborator.
acceptance_criteria: Measured on a short test5 segment: the pruned fraction X/Y at prune_abstol=1e-16, the colour count (residual evaluations per Jacobian build) pruned vs unpruned, and wall-clock, Jacobian builds and failure count for both. A statement of whether regime (a) is a free win, and if so whether the BOUT++ default should change.

title: Per-merge trigger and the regression rule for the standing watch
description:
perf-bisect became a standing watch on 2026-08-01: it gains a rung as each PR lands on master, rather than being a one-off backward ladder. That needs two things the current design does not have.

A trigger. What fires a rung when a PR merges, how the commit is picked up, and what happens when several land close together. Batching is probably right - a rung per day of merges rather than per merge - but that is a decision, not an assumption.

A regression rule that survives uncontrolled loading. A watch that fires whenever a PR lands cannot choose its slot or its neighbours, so it must gate on work counts, not wall clock. F17 settled that already: wall clock carries a tens-of-percent communications term, F22 puts the concurrency penalty at 10%, and the first ladder pass demonstrates it directly - nonlinear iterations across the five measured anchors were 4541, 4542, 4563, 4546, 4541, inside 0.5%, while wall time spanned 2409-2751 s and tracked launch order rather than commit age. Counts were the signal; wall clock was noise.

So the rule gates on nl_its and ncalls against the previous rung, with a threshold set from the 1D case own repeat scatter once that exists (so-v3o). Do not reuse test4steady 2 percent figure - it is a different case.

Depends on the 1D test, because the per-merge cadence is only affordable there.
acceptance_criteria: A written trigger and threshold rule, and a rung that fires from a merge without being launched by hand.

title: Turn on diagnose_failures and name the 661 failures
description:
The cheapest missing measurement in the whole project, and every run so far has had it off.

solver:diagnose_failures = 0 on all four short-test runs. PETSc records the reason for each failure and snes.cxx:812 will print it along with the min/max of every field and its ddt. Line search collapse, iteration limit, and NaN point at three completely different fixes, and nothing currently distinguishes them.

Affordable: solver_fails_max was 7 against a cap of 20 on test5steady, so the run has plenty of headroom to carry the diagnostics. Cost is log volume only.

Do this before or alongside the other experiments here - without it, a failure count that moves cannot be attributed.
acceptance_criteria: test5steady rerun with diagnose_failures = true, and a breakdown of the failures by PETSc reason.
notes:
ANSWERED 2026-08-01 from the CVODE-like scan's baseline, which is the first case in this project ever to set diagnose_failures = true.

Full run, all 731 failures:
  reason -9  SNES_DIVERGED_DTOL     412  (56%)  residual GREW past the divergence tolerance
  reason -5  SNES_DIVERGED_MAX_IT   319  (44%)  ran out of the 10 Newton iterations

An early 39-failure sample read 72% MAX_IT / 28% DTOL. Over the full run it is the other way round, so do not quote the early split.

DTOL is the headline. PETSc's divergence tolerance defaults to 1e4 times the initial residual, so on the majority of failures the Newton step did not merely fail to converge - it made the residual four orders of magnitude worse. That is violent divergence from a single full undamped step, not slow progress.

Nothing at -6 SNES_DIVERGED_LINE_SEARCH, and that is structural rather than informative: with snes_linesearch_type = basic there is no line search that can fail. Nothing at -3 linear-solve failure and nothing at -4 NaN either, so the LU and the residual evaluation are both healthy.

Consequence: the problem is purely the length of the Newton step being attempted, and a line search is aimed straight at the dominant mode. This raises so-zk3 above the controller work in expected value, which is not where the analysis had it.

Supporting number from the same run: 399 of 517 accepted steps converged in ONE Newton iteration, so the controller sat at its maximum growth factor for 77% of steps.

description:
The structural fix for test5 cost, and it attacks the 84 percent.

PETSc split on test5steady SNES-MUMPS-2: finite-difference colouring 84.0%, LU numeric factorisation 11.3%, Krylov solve 1.7%, genuine residual evaluations 1.8%. The LU is already perfect - lin_its equals nl_its in every one of the 470 accepted steps, one Krylov iteration per Newton iteration. There is no preconditioner improvement available. All the cost is BUILDING the operator: 2406 Jacobian builds at about 160 residual evaluations each, 421 residual evaluations per Newton iteration.

This is also the answer to why CVODE stays within 2x with only a conduction preconditioner: it never builds a Jacobian.

The change: matrix_free_operator = true with lag_jacobian raised to 20-50. The Newton operator becomes an exact directional derivative at one residual evaluation per Krylov vector; the assembled LU-factorised Jacobian is demoted to preconditioner only, so it can be lagged hard without hurting Newton convergence. That is CVODE architecture with a much better preconditioner.

Arithmetic against the current 385k evaluations: 24 builds at lag_jacobian=20 is 3.8k, plus 913 Newton iterations at even 20 Krylov vectors each is 18k. Large enough margin to absorb being badly wrong about the Krylov count.

Not a new design - SNES-1 and SNES-PTC-1 already run matrix_free_operator = true. Prepare it as a MUMPS variant.

Risk to watch: directional derivatives on a non-smooth residual (van Albada limiter, floors, softFloor) can be noisy in the differencing parameter. The FD-coloured Jacobian is equally inconsistent there, so this is not obviously worse, but watch lin_its per Newton iteration - if it explodes, the lagged preconditioner is the problem, not the operator.
acceptance_criteria: Measured on test5steady against the SNES-MUMPS-2 row: Jacobian builds, RHS evaluations, wall, and lin_its per nl_it. Physics compared against the same baseline.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01 on test5steady, and the recommendation in this issue is WRONG for this configuration. Matrix-free loses badly, and the reason is the very thing this issue cited as the opportunity.

                          wall    ncalls   nl_its   lin_its  fails   jac   t_jac  t_ksp
  step2 assembled lag3     208 s   133986    1204      1204     96    803   0.805  0.014
  matrix-free lag5        2038 s  1005985    2351    107924   1226   3528   0.362  0.570
  matrix-free lag20 *     2410 s  1203930    5813    216471   1070   4189   0.363  0.569
  * also carried the tightened tolerance, so confounded; lag5 is the clean test.

The architecture change did exactly what was predicted: Jacobian construction fell from 0.805 to 0.362 of the run. It still lost by 10x, because Krylov replaced it at 0.570.

The mechanism, and it is the flaw in the original reasoning. With the assembled Jacobian and exact MUMPS LU, lin_its EQUALS nl_its - 1204 and 1204, one Krylov iteration per Newton iteration. That is the theoretical optimum for a linear solve and it cannot be improved on. The LU is an exact inverse of the ASSEMBLED Jacobian; the moment the operator becomes the true matrix-free Jacobian, the preconditioner stops being exact and GMRES has to iterate - 46 iterations per Newton iteration at lag 5, each costing a full residual evaluation. Lagging harder makes the preconditioner staler and it gets worse, not better.

This issue reasoned that 84% in Jacobian construction was the opportunity and the 1.7% Krylov share was proof preconditioning had nothing left to give. Both halves were right and the conclusion drawn from them was wrong: the 1.7% is small BECAUSE the Jacobian is assembled and exactly factorised. The cost and the optimality are the same fact, and you cannot keep one without the other.

There is also a secondary cascade: matrix-free raised failures to 1226, and a failure forces a Jacobian rebuild and resets the lag (snes.cxx:857), so builds went UP to 3528 despite lag 5 against lag 3.

What survives. The lever is to build the assembled Jacobian LESS OFTEN, not to stop building it - which F18 already showed is safe (lag 1 to 3 on test4steady, -58% with an identical trajectory). Branch C is running that sweep now at lag 5, 10 and 20 on the best configuration.

The test4steady isolation described in the original issue is now moot for matrix-free; retarget it at the assembled lag sweep if a clean isolation is still wanted.

title: Flash-driven solver cost on test5
description:
The perftest-side workstream on the core flashes: what they cost the solver on test5, and what removes that cost. Distinct from the cf tracker at notebooks/ai-diagnose/core-flashes, which owns the physics diagnosis on the st40 cases. Read that projects investigation_notes.md before starting anything here.

Why this epic exists. Analysis on 2026-08-01 tied the test5 SNES failures to the flash mechanism diagnosed in the cf project: electron parallel conduction acting on derived Te = Pe/Ne, with kappa_par_e enormous in hot weakly collisional cells, converting sub-resolution Te corrugations into large ddt(Pe) sources.

What the store data supports:
- Ranking the four short tests by T^2.5/n at the outboard separatrix gives test4stiff 1x (0 failures), test4steady 11x (0), test5steady 1300x (661), test5stiff 28000x (245). The two failure-free tests are 100-3000x less stiff in electron conduction.
- test5 runs with the electron conduction flux limiter OFF (e:kappa_limit_alpha = -1); both test4s have it at 0.2. That limiter is the only cap on kappa_par (braginskii_conduction.cxx:252).
- On the identical test5steady case, SNES carries max|ddt(Pe)| 11x larger than CVODE and 5x more localised (max/rms 18.1 against 3.8).
- Loosening atol/rtol raises the fluctuations 35x on peak and 16x on RMS, measured controlled on test4steady across the one tolerance step of the MUMPS-1 to MUMPS-2 scan.
- The flashes cost CVODE its timestep directly: Spearman 0.89 between max|ddt(Pe)| and RHS evaluations per output interval on test5stiff. They do not time SNES failures (Spearman -0.37 and 0.07), because SNES has no time error control. The flash sets how high the wall is; the timestep controller decides how often SNES walks into it.

Two kinds of work hang off this, and they should not be confused:
- Make SNES survive the flash: matrix-free operator, controller, tolerance, line search. These do not change the answer.
- Establish that the flash is what sets the ceiling: cap kappa, turn the limiter on. These DO change the answer, so they are diagnostics, not speedups.

Ruled out already, do not reopen without new evidence: limiting at cell centres rather than faces (test5 has no limiter and is the case that fails); conduction reconstruction (ProductJK and Harmonic both tried, no performance change - they change how kappa is averaged to faces, not how large it is).
notes:
SCAN COMPLETE 2026-08-01. Nine runs on test5steady, one build, sequential and alone. Result: two settings on SNES-MUMPS-2 give 3.25x, and SNES is 6.0x faster than CVODE-2 on the test where it was believed to lose.

  target_its = 5              (was 100, against max_nonlinear_iterations = 10)
  snes_linesearch_type = bt   (was basic)
  676 s -> 208 s, CVODE-2 1249 s, peak target Te moves 0.002%

Cumulative ladder: baseline 676, +target_its 432, +bt 208, +tight tolerance 2071, +matrix-free 2410.
Lag sweep on the best configuration: lag 3/5/10/20 = 208/212/241/250 s.

Three routes at the 84% Jacobian share are measured and closed - tolerance, matrix-free, and lagging - see F29 and the corrected F27. The single most useful correction: the 84% is not a cost with a lever behind it, because lin_its equals nl_its exactly and that optimum exists BECAUSE the Jacobian is assembled and exactly factorised.

Open, in order: the line-search scan (so-erp), the count-scatter question (so-xi1), and whether these two settings transfer to test4 and to test2.

Everything extracted and validated; no case directories deleted; nothing committed.

title: perf-bisect: define the test — truncated test2scratch on SNES-MUMPS-1
description: The steady/stiff tests restart from a fixed base/ state produced by one build; run under an old commit that state is no longer its equilibrium, so timing mixes solver speed with seed drift. A from-scratch run has no seed at all, which removes the confound. test2scratch at nout=450 (45 ms) took 56 m 36 s on 2026-06-12 under SNES-MUMPS-1. Choose an nout that costs about 30 min on today's build, by measuring once - the from-scratch transient is the expensive part, so cost is not linear in nout. Fix nout and simulated duration across the ladder and measure wall time; never fix wall time. SNES-MUMPS-1 is the recipe: the user confirms it has been in play across the whole window. Open question: is one recipe enough, or does a CVODE arm belong here too, given a change could help one solver and hurt the other?
close_reason:
Settled 2026-07-31. The test is test2scratch at nout = 200, SNES-MUMPS-1, MC build, slot 1.

The user chose 20 ms of simulated time rather than a wall-clock target, which is the better axis anyway: the work is fixed and the wall time is the measurement. The input steps at 95788 * 0.1, i.e. 0.1 ms per output, so today's nout = 450 is 45 ms and nout = 200 is 20 ms. No calibration run is needed, which also sidesteps having to calibrate on a VanAlbada build for an MC ladder.

Expect appreciably more than 20/45 of the full 56 m 36 s, because the from-scratch transient is front-loaded rather than uniform. From scratch also means no seed state, so the restart-drift confound that rules out the steady and stiff tests does not apply here.

One recipe, SNES-MUMPS-1: the user confirmed it has been in play across the whole window. A second CVODE arm remains possible - a change can help one solver and hurt the other - but is not being taken now.

title: perf-bisect: does the oldest anchor still build? (window feasibility)
description: Everything else in perf-bisect depends on how far back the ladder can reach, so probe before designing. hermes-3 pins BOUT++ as a submodule (bumped 10 times in the last 12 months), so each commit carries its own BOUT++; PETSc does not follow, and comes from the spack hermes3 env at 3.23.3. A year-old BOUT++ against PETSc 3.23.3 is the most likely build failure. Take the oldest candidate anchor, build it in a fresh clone/worktree outside /home/mike/work/hermes-3, and record what happens. Open question: if it fails, is the answer to shorten the window, or to pin an older PETSc per epoch? Shortening is cheaper and probably right, but the failure mode decides.
close_reason:
Probed 2026-07-31. The 12-month window is feasible: the oldest anchor a35e2f5e (2025-08-27), carrying BOUT++ c4c149a2 (2025-08-13), builds and links against spack PETSc 3.23.3. FindPETSc's MULTIPASS_TEST_3 succeeds and CMake reports PETSc support: ON. Warnings-as-errors was also a non-issue: 7 warnings, all in BOUT-dev headers, none fatal with HERMES_ERROR_ON_WARNINGS=ON.

The build did fail first time, but not for either reason expected. HERMES_SLOPE_LIMITER=VanAlbada is not buildable at that commit: FV::VanAlbada entered BOUT++ on 2026-06-11, so it exists for only the last two of the twelve anchors. FV::MC has existed since 2017. Rebuilt with -s MC: clean, hermes-3 executable produced, 0 errors. See the ladder issue for the consequence.

Note the failure shape for the driver: CMake accepted the VanAlbada option and generated a config header naming a type that did not exist, so it failed at 82% of the compile, not at configure. Checking configure output alone would have called it a success.

title: Campaign claims store-independence but still loads case directories
description:
analysis-solver-opt.py's docstring says this campaign reads the results store and never a dump, which is the whole reason it exists separately - so its reports keep building after R8 deletes the run directories. The campaign-local pages do read bundles. But Campaign.run_cases still resolves every study case against case_root and raises MissingCase if the directory is gone.

Hit 2026-07-30: the six R20 noise runs were extracted, validated and deleted as R22 licenses. A study referencing one of them then failed to build. The store has everything that study needed; only the loader disagreed.

So the promise is not kept, and the failure mode is bad - it appears only once a directory is deleted, which is exactly when the store is supposed to take over, and it makes deleting runs unsafe in practice while R22 says it is safe.

Needs a decision on which pages genuinely require dump data. If some do, the campaign should load bundles for the rest and say clearly which pages cannot be drawn from a bundle. If none do, the loader should read the store.
acceptance_criteria: A study referencing only extracted-and-deleted runs builds its PDF from the store alone, or the campaign states per page which need dumps and skips them with a visible note.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-07-31. CaseLoader gained an optional dir_fallback: a callable name -> path, tried only when no directory exists under case_root. dir() prefers the live case directory and falls back to it; missing() counts a case missing only when neither resolves; case() distinguishes the two failures, so asking for a dataset on a record-only case says the record holds text and not datasets rather than 'directory not found'. Campaign gained needs_dumps (default True, so the physics campaign is untouched) which skips the eager pre-load that opened every dataset for nothing.

case_comparison learned nothing about the perftest store: the fallback is a plain callable and the solver-opt campaign supplies bundle_for(), keeping campaign-specific knowledge in the campaign file.

Verified: study 2 builds with no dataset loads at all, using a run whose directory was deleted; study 1 rebuilds; the physics campaign's study 3 rebuilds and still loads dumps as before; and all four resolution paths were exercised directly, including both error messages.

title: Residual conclusions before 2026-07-30 were guard-cell garbage (F20)
description:
The resid_* fields hold up to 1e15 in the radial guard cells against 1e-3 interior. Every residual share computed before the extractor fix summed them in, so which equation 'holds the solver up' was answered by whose guard cells were worst: Pe 95% contaminated, versus Pd 74% / Pe 26% interior-only, and NVd/NVd+ rather than Pe on the scale_vars runs.

The six test4steady runs are re-extracted and correct. What is NOT checked: every other analysis that read these fields, including the residual_norm_postprocessing showcase notebook, which uses the raw sum and whose published conclusions are therefore suspect. Also unchecked: whether snes_local_residual has the same problem, and whether BOUT++ should be zeroing those cells at source rather than every reader trimming them.

Relates to the neutral-pressure-spike issue: with guards excluded, Pd genuinely does dominate the MUMPS-1 runs.
notes:
Showcase notebook checked 2026-07-31: its conclusions are SAFE. Shares are identical raw versus masked to the digit on both its cases — MC Pe 86.32%/Pd 13.46%, VanAlbada Pe 72.03%/Pd 26.97% — because the guard cells on those two runs hold 5.47e-310, a denormal that underflows to zero when squared. It was right by luck rather than by reasoning: freshly-allocated pages come from the OS zeroed, and only reused memory carries garbage, which is why the same field is clean on one run and 1e15 on another.

Its reduction code has been corrected to mask explicitly via clear_guards so it no longer rests on that. The edit could NOT be executed: the notebook imports a helper module (perftests/analysis.py) that no longer exists and was never in git. Filed separately. Stored outputs left in place and remain valid, since the numbers are provably unchanged.

Trap written into hermes-oracle/docs/postprocessing.md, next to the other guard-cell traps, including the two sub-traps: which fields are affected varies run to run, and this applies only to the resid_ diagnostics, not to evolved fields whose guards carry boundary conditions.

Decided: no BOUT++ source fix. The extractor already masks and refuses to proceed without a mask, and R8 deletes the dumps, so the exposure is bounded to ad-hoc readers — which the doc note now covers.
close_reason:
All three open items resolved.

snes_local_residual is clean, and so is snes_global_residual: the resid_ fields use emptyFrom() (snes.cxx:391-394) which allocates without initialising, while local_residual is explicitly zeroed (snes.cxx:448). Measured guard max exactly 0.0 against 7.6e6 for resid_Pe. So resid_final, resid_drop and resid_per_rhs in every index row are sound.

Every other reader enumerated: five files reference resid_. Three read bundle tables or column names only (perftest/index.py, perftest/store.py, analysis-solver-opt.py) and so consume already-masked data. Two notebooks read raw dump fields, and both are unaffected — residual_norm_postprocessing (MC Pe 86.32/Pd 13.46, VanAlbada 72.03/26.97) and scale_vars_residual_weighting (no-scale_vars Pe 86.2/Pd 13.7, scale_vars Pe 57.2/NVd+ 19.5/Pd 19.1), identical raw and masked in both. Their cases hold denormals (~5.5e-310) in the guards rather than garbage, because freshly-allocated pages arrive from the OS zeroed.

No BOUT++ source fix, by decision. The extractor masks and refuses to run without a mask; R8 deletes the dumps; the trap is documented in hermes-oracle/docs/postprocessing.md for ad-hoc readers.

Loose end, not blocking: scale_vars_residual_weighting.ipynb still asserts 'Guard cells are checked to be zero below, so summing the full array is safe' and checks only resid_Pe using index slicing rather than clear_guards. Its numbers are right today and its reasoning is not. It is untracked in-progress work, so it was left alone rather than edited.

title: First results table and plots (R11)
description:
The user wants to see the results as a table, and some first plots, before any solver physics work. R11 outranks everything else: if a result cannot be presented digestibly it is not finished.

Read the index only, never case directories or dumps. Analysis belongs in the campaign script per the perftests conventions, with anything campaign-specific in a local page function rather than edited into the shared case_comparison package.

Honest scope, and this must be stated on the output: these are descriptive. No difference shown can yet be called an improvement, because the noise floor has not been measured. Show what was run, what it cost and where the time went — not which recipe wins.
acceptance_criteria: A table of recorded runs plus first plots, produced from the index alone, carrying the caveat that no difference is yet established as real.
close_reason:
Delivered as a study rather than a loose table: analysis-perftests.py now carries test4_mumps1_to_mumps2, emitting output/05_test4_mumps1_to_mumps2.pdf. Four pages — provenance cover, cost-per-step table, per-run evolution histories, and the log_view time breakdown.

Scope changed from the original description in two ways, both for the better. It reads the BUNDLES, not just the index, because 'how things evolved' needs the per-step histories and those are what survive R8 deletion. And it no longer needs the old on-disk runs, which the user is discarding, so the blocker on bulk extraction was stale and removed.

The plotting pages are campaign-local in analysis-perftests.py per the conventions; the store reader is general and went to sdtools as perftest/store.py.

title: Extract every run still on disk into the store
description:
About 30 case directories sit in test4dev and test5dev, roughly 52 GB. They are the only runs that exist, and several are the evidence behind current findings. Extracting them populates the index with real rows so the first table and plots have something to describe.

Not all will extract cleanly and that is the point: runs launched before the tee convention have no console, so no log_view, no options_left and no PETSc version. Those rows come out thinner and the report says which. Record what is there, flag what is missing, do not invent.

Order matters: run after the extractor has tests, since this writes many rows at once and a silent bug would be copied across all of them. Dumps still exist so a re-extraction is possible, which is what makes this recoverable.
acceptance_criteria: Every case directory on disk is either extracted with a validated report, or listed with the reason it could not be.
notes:
Open question for the next session, 2026-07-30: the user said they would rather start from scratch and discard the old runs than extract them. If that stands, this issue should be CANCELLED rather than done — the 18 legacy rows already preserve those runs' wall times in the index, and extracting the dumps would only add cost breakdowns for runs nobody intends to compare against again.

What is NOT recoverable if the dumps go: ncalls, the time breakdown, residuals and physics for those runs. The index keeps wall time only. The long test5 scratch runs are 6-34 h each and cannot be casually remade; the short ones can.

Six test4steady runs from 2026-07-30 ARE extracted and validated (state=recorded), so those case directories are safe to delete whenever the space is wanted — about 2.5 GB of the 55 GB in cases/perftests.
close_reason:
CANCELLED 2026-07-31 by the user's decision: runs made before this project are separate work, to be redone and deleted, and are never to be extracted. The 43 unextracted directories in test2dev/test4dev/test5dev are not a backlog — they are not this project's runs.

Replaced by the standing rule that the index defines what exists: a run is part of this project iff it has an index row, and no tool or agent should enumerate case directories to find work. BOUT.log.console is the physical marker, since it exists only for runs launched under the tee convention — 22 directories have one, 41 do not, and all 19 project rows carry one.

title: Create the index and migrate the 18 legacy rows (R6/R7)
description:
The store has a README, a schema and an empty runs/. It has no index, so the extractor's first write would create one and the real results still live in the legacy 14-column run_records.csv. Two ledgers alive at once is the temporary state the project CLAUDE.md warns about, and it ends here.

Migrate the 18 legacy rows into the new schema rather than archiving them: they are the evidence behind F1, F2 and F5. Fields the old rows cannot supply (RHS counts, cores, CHECK level, slot, outcome, epoch) are recorded empty — never guessed, since empty means unknown and a guess becomes a conclusion nobody re-checks.

Column order is currently defined in sdtools perftest/index.py INDEX_COLUMNS, 51 columns, meaning-first. Check it against schema.md and make one of them authoritative.
acceptance_criteria: index.tsv exists in the store with the 18 legacy rows migrated, no invented values, and run_records.csv marked superseded.
close_reason:
index.tsv exists in the store with all 18 legacy rows migrated: 51 columns, 14 populated, 37 empty and correctly so. Nothing guessed — run_time_str dropped as a duplicate, hermes_commit_date as recoverable from the commit. run_records.csv marked superseded in both CLAUDE.md files and takes no new rows; recording instructions now point at extract_test.py.

Three schema gaps found and documented: state gains 'legacy' (no bundle, never validated, must not read as a measurement of the same standard); test_id is not unique because two runs of one test can start in the same second in different slots, so the later takes a -2 suffix; concurrency left empty on legacy rows because the old ledger may not list every concurrent run, making any count a lower bound. perftest/index.py INDEX_COLUMNS declared the authoritative column list.

Byproduct worth more than the migration: F15 — the three June baselines all ran concurrently.

title: Build the record extractor
description:
Missing piece: nothing yet turns a finished case directory into a record. Reads a case dir, writes the per-test bundle into perftest-results/runs/<test_id>/ and appends one row to the index per schema.md, then reports whether the extraction validated so the directory can be deleted (R22).

Lives in sdtools, not the results repo and not the read-only hermes-perftest template — it is useful to any Hermes-3 performance work.

Inputs: BOUT.inp, BOUT.settings, BOUT.log.0, the captured console (log_view, options_left, snes_view, ksp_view, petsc_version), the dumps for RunMetrics and solver counters, and the resid_ fields for the derived metrics.

Reuse rather than rewrite: hermes3/logparse.py already parses log_view tables; cmonitor.py:279-318 already parses the SNES log lines; case_comparison/provenance.py already extracts commits and merged options. Read dumps through xhermes, never raw xbout/xarray.

Needs the user's explicit go-ahead before any code is written.
acceptance_criteria: A finished case directory becomes a validated bundle plus one index row, with a clear pass/fail on whether the directory is safe to delete.
notes: Design settled 2026-07-29. The index is declared before the run, not written after it: a row carries six intent fields (case_dir, test, recipe, varied, epoch, note) and the extractor fills the rest, joining on case_dir with at most one open row per directory. seed, slot and concurrency are measured, not declared. Bundle holds raw files plus three parsed tables (per output step, per PETSc event, residual metrics) so analysis never parses text. See perftest-results/schema.md for the lifecycle and rules. Residual metric design (so-r53.6) does not block: extractor ships without it and is re-run on bundles later, at the cost of losing per-equation fields for any run extracted first.
close_reason:
Built and validated in sdtools: perftest/ (extract.py, index.py, recipe.py) plus cli/extract_test.py, with the text parsing in hermes3/logparse.py. A finished case directory becomes a bundle plus one filled index row, and the report's pass/fail is what licenses deleting the dumps.

Verified on real runs: 39 of 51 columns filled on a completed test4steady, and the log_view time shares match F13 independently (jac 0.775, pcsetup 0.151, ksp 0.0095, func 0.0071). A failed run extracts too, classified snes_failure from the '======== SNES failed =========' marker, with sim_time_ms 0.0 recording that it got nowhere. Console trimming drops repeated PETSc object dumps (681 on one run, including 324 PC Object blocks that a fixed SNES/KSP marker list missed), taking the bundle from 2.2 MB to 244 KB and matching the store's stated budget while leaving log_view, options_left and the first block of each object type intact.

Three schema columns are computed that were not in the original plan: hermes_branch from the sdrun banner (better than asking git which branches contain a commit), diffs by comparing the case's [solver]/[petsc] sections against the named recipe, and concurrency as a pass over the whole index after each extraction, since a run that overlapped this one may be recorded later.

Left empty deliberately: ne_sep/te_sep, which need a separatrix location convention this being a connected double null with four midplanes (so-joa); and the finer outcome classes beyond completed/snes_failure, which is schema.md's own open question.

title: Measure log_view overhead, resid_ disk cost, options_left behaviour
description: Three numbers the capture set needs before it goes on every run. (1) Does log_view slow a run? PETSc accumulates timings whether or not it prints, so the marginal cost should be near zero, but it goes on every run so measure once rather than assume. (2) Disk cost of the seven resid_ fields per output step on a long run — transient since extraction precedes deletion, but three runs share the machine so peak disk matters. (3) Does options_left actually flag unused options on the installed PETSc version? It matters because [petsc] has no whitelist, so a misspelled option is silently ignored and a recipe can quietly not do what it says. All three are cheap: short tests, and (3) can be provoked deliberately with a nonsense option.
acceptance_criteria: Three measured numbers or behaviours, recorded in findings, with the capture set updated if any surprises.
close_reason: All three measured on nine test4steady runs. (1) log_view and the other PETSc options cost 1-2 s on a 155 s run, inside the 2 s spread between identical controls — free. (2) resid_ fields cost 28 MB per 90 output steps, 393 to 421 MB, about 7%. (3) options_left works and immediately flagged snes_fd_color_use_mat, set in three recipes, as never used (F12). Bonus: 1.3% run-to-run spread at single loading, and PETSc 3.23.3 readable from the console.

title: Solver behaviour puzzles
description: Investigations into why the solvers behave as they do, as opposed to tuning settings. Findings here feed the optimisation rather than being optimisation themselves. Deliverables are hermes-oracle reports (reports/ directory convention), not just issue comments.

title: Phase 3: decide the capture set (R9)
description: Decisions taken 2026-07-29: solver:diagnose=true goes on every run (it gates both the SNES iteration counts in the log and the resid_ fields in the dump). Scope is SNES only for now (R26). Instrumentation overhead is accepted — relative improvements remain valid — with one caveat to respect when choosing options: prefer diagnostics whose cost does not scale with the quantity being measured, since a per-KSP-iteration monitor costs more on exactly the recipes that take more iterations and would bias the comparison. Promoting SNES counts into dump variables is wanted but explicitly must not block: first establish what can be extracted from the console and log alone, then judge whether the C++ change is worth it. Remaining work: write the core set and the extended set, and decide which PETSc monitor options are affordable.
acceptance_criteria: A written core set and extended set, each item justified, with the console-and-log-only route established first.
close_reason: Capture set agreed 2026-07-30 and written up in capture-set.md as the spec the extractor is built against. Core set, extended set and not-captured list all justified; console-and-log-only route established first (SNES counts stay a non-blocking wish). Both open questions settled: disk cost measured at full scratch length (6.6% of the dump, 0.4 GiB across three concurrent runs, against 79 GB free) rather than extrapolated, and bundle tables are TSV at full float precision, matching the index schema.

title: Capture stdout at launch so log_view reports survive (F6)
description: PETSc writes its log_view profiling report to stdout at finalize; sdrun.py ends in execvp so stdout goes wherever the shell sent it, and nothing captures it. Zero reports exist on disk despite log_view being active in three recipes. acceptance_criteria: A launched run leaves a parseable log_view report in its case directory, and logparse.py reads it.
notes:
Proposed mechanism. Runs launch from $cases/runplanN.sh in screens h1-h3 as 'echo y | sdrun.py -s=N -p=exe -d case'; sdrun execs into mpirun so stdout goes to the screen and is lost.

Change: append '2>&1 | tee <case>/BOUT.log.console' to each runplan line.

Why that filename: reset_test.py deletes BOUT.dmp.*, BOUT.log.* and *.pid (reset_test.py:29). Naming it BOUT.log.console means the existing reset sweeps it automatically, so a stale console file cannot survive into the next test in a reused directory. It also avoids the numbered-log parsers, which match BOUT.log.\d+ and will ignore it. Minor side effect: caseplan's n_logs count gains one.

Why tee rather than plain redirection: keeps the live view in the screen, which matters for monitoring. This is a stdout pipe and is categorically different from the 'yes | runplan' stdin incident of 2026-07-20 that OOM-killed a run — that filled mpirun's stdin buffer without bound; this writes mpirun's stdout to a file. Worth stating explicitly in the skill so nobody conflates them.

Known downside to verify: piping makes stdout a pipe rather than a tty, so libc block-buffers instead of line-buffering and the live screen view becomes chunky. Mitigate with 'stdbuf -oL' if it proves annoying. sdrun.py's only tty check is cosmetic (Style(sys.stdout.isatty()), sdrun.py:250).

Rows are now split from the right by the 20 known columns instead of hardcoded character widths, which also fixes event names containing spaces. That is five anchors - 2026-02, 03, 04, 06, 07 - out of a twelve-month window. Everything from the 2026-01 anchor backwards collapses its timestep inside the first output interval and aborts, so the older half is unmeasurable rather than measured-and-flat. Across the five measured anchors the solver work is flat: nonlinear iterations 4541, 4542, 4563, 4546, 4541 and failure counts 1213, 1213, 1224, 1219, 1213, all inside 0.5%. title: (R19) No input sets diagnose_failures, so only the last SNES failure is recorded
description:
The run-case skill requires solver:diagnose_failures = true in every input, so
that BOUT++ prints a block for every SNES failure rather than only the last
one. No input in this project sets it: the test4 cases set solver:diagnose =
true and leave diagnose_failures at its default of 0.

Found while classifying the ten runs that diverged on
kspsetinitialguessnonzero the night of 2026-09-22. Those were still
classifiable, because each hit the same failure twenty times and the last block
told the whole story. A run whose failures change character would be recorded
with only its final one, and the recipe then looks innocent.

reaches new cases rather than being patched per run. Nothing already recorded
can be recovered: the option changes what a run prints while it runs.

would bloat BOUT.log.0 on a run that fails often, and that log is read in full

title: (R11) Study setup cost grows with studies: study grammar, one queue, settings-only config
description:
Why. Setting up study 3 on 2026-09-22 took the agent about 25 minutes, and the user asked whether the project scales to thousands of runs and tens of studies. The review found the run machinery scales (per-run setup cost is zero, runner idempotent, index locked) but the study-authoring and record layer does not: the cost is per study and per decision, and it is text that agents load whole at every session start (about 2850 lines today, growing about 100 lines of runlog per study).

Evidence from the study 3 diffs: 103 hand-written [[variant]] blocks over 707 lines, each with a note and the same three base overrides; the plan written in five places (study headers, runlog, approval scope, manifest, handoff memo); campaign.toml is 127 comment lines against 90 of settings; slot partitioning and the cross-file duplicate check done by hand because the runner takes one study per slot; repeat top-ups sized by hand.

Proposed, in order of payoff. The user has not chosen which yet; propose diffs for the phrase before each.
1. Study grammar: a base override table, a grid product and a repeats_to top-up in perftest/runner.py load_study. The 103 blocks become about 15.
2. One queue across slots: any slot's driver claims the next unsettled trial from one study list, so slot balancing and the duplicate check disappear.
3. Settings files hold settings only; history moves to the runlog, which owns it. The approval scope points at the manifest instead of restating it.
4. The manifest is the one description of a study; the runlog entry and the handoff memo point at it in a few lines.
5. A --plan mode on run_campaign.py printing cells, windows, repeats, top-ups needed and hours per slot.
6. Rule on the requirements candidates (237 lines, rounds 3-10, one open since 2026-07-30) or move them to the tracker.

Do not touch the runner or campaign.toml while drivers are running. Blocked on the study 3 report because the report reads the record as it is.
notes:
Direction added 2026-09-22 evening, from the user: the studies so far are pilots. Future studies run several days, and the user wants to try unsupervised study creation (the agent writes the next study from the last one's results) at thousands of runs per study. That raises two items and reorders the list. One queue across slots (item 2) and the study grammar (item 1) become preconditions, because a generated study must be a small data structure the runner can take whole. New item 7: a generated, compact state the agent loads instead of the prose record, so the loop of read results, write study, launch fits in one context; the cells table and manifest are the start. New item 8: multi-day operation, budget in days, disk prune proven over days, runner restart without a handoff memo. design.md section 9 already names the optimiser interface this feeds.
RULED 2026-09-24 on multi-day operation (item 8): daily baseline control cell per window, speeds compared only against the same day's baseline: yes. Deferred as less important: auto-restart via systemd user services with crash-loop stop, heartbeat file and status check, drivers from a pinned worktree with the commit per row, budget stated as slots plus end time, alert channel, slot share. Not rejected, just later.

The open question is where it belongs: the run-case skill already owns the rule
