title: [bug] Dependency check refuses a valid override when the space spells the condition as a comma list
description:
The dependency check in perftest/runner.py refuses a valid override when the
search space writes the condition as a prose list.

depends_met understands a bool, a name, "not <name>" and "<a> or <b>". It does
not understand "1, 2 or 3", which is how search-space.toml spells the condition
on petsc:mat_mumps_cntl_7: the matcher splits on " or " and compares against
["1, 2", "3"], so a run that sets petsc:mat_mumps_icntl_35 = 1 is refused with
the message that the setting cannot take effect.

Found by the dry run of study 3 on 2026-09-22. The block low-rank cell now runs
at the MUMPS default threshold instead, so the study lost the threshold, not the
cell.

Same family as the lag_jacobian refusal of 2026-09-21, which was the space
spelling an unset knob as prose. Both say the same thing: the space is written
for a human reader and the checker parses it as data, with no test holding the
two spellings together.

Two ways out, and the choice is the open question: teach the matcher comma
lists, or forbid prose in a depends value and make the space use a list. The
second needs a sweep of every depends entry in the space and a test that fails
on anything the matcher cannot parse.

title: (F: core-edge residual) Investigation 01: why the residual norm sits in a few inboard core-edge cells
description:
First investigation once the investigation record kind is accepted (see the report-rules issue). Question: why does the SNES residual norm sit in under ten core-edge cells on every test4 run, and what decides which cells?

State on 2026-09-22 evening (findings entry "The residual norm sits at the core edge all run long" in campaigns/test4-jacobian/findings.md; notes below): item (2) of the plan is done. Across the six 100 ms runs the norm sits in the first five interior radial cells at the core boundary at every output. Through the 2-10 ms transient the neutral equations hold it at the OUTBOARD midplane core edge (theta 72-80; the earlier "inboard" label was wrong), where Nd/Nnorm is within a factor of a few of the rtol = 1e-5 scaling floor and the dump residual fields are the scaled residual. From 12 ms on Pe holds 0.98-1.00 of it beside the X-points, at the domain's maximum pressure, no floor involved. 78-91 per cent of the Newton iterations fall in the neutral phase.

The link to test: the scale_vars floor bug (scale_vars floors elements below rtol, amplifying their residual by up to 1/rtol). The core-edge neutral cells look like that floor seen from the dumps. What would settle it: (1) per-element scale factors from a diagnose run, to measure the floored elements' share of the norm directly (the follow-up issue under the bug); (2) one 4.0-4.1 ms baseline run with the floor moved (a different rtol, or the per-field floor fix) to see whether the residual leaves those cells; (3) the code read of the neutral core boundary (bndry_core = free_o3) and the diffusion limiter at low density, now second in priority. Cost: (1) is a log read; (2) is one short run through a campaign study file with approval; (3) is hours of reading.

Why it matters: the solver's convergence test is decided by those cells through the phase where most of the cost is, so every setting in the campaign was measured against them. A floor fix changes what everything is measured against.
notes:
2026-09-22 evening: the investigation record kind exists. The directory investigations/I01-2026-09-22-core-edge-residual/ in the store holds investigation.toml and brief.md (question, where seen, what would settle it, why it matters); data/ is empty and report.py is not written. The register reports/README.md lists it as open. Both S01 and S02 point at it from their cells sections. S02's 4.0-5.0 ms map adds a fact for the brief: on that window lag 1 alone puts the norm below the midplane and the gains above it, and the neutral pressure residual sits one radial cell further out than on the 0.1 ms window.
2026-09-22, later: correction to the note above and the report built. After the neutral phase the norm passes to the PLASMA equations, not to Pe alone: under lag 1 Pe holds 0.98-1.00 from 12 ms on; under the baseline Pe and NVd+ trade it output by output until about 40 ms, then Pe alone. The Newton-work shares are by the end of the neutral phase (12 ms): 0.92-0.93 baseline, 0.79/0.71/0.56 lag 1. Report: reports/investigations/I01-2026-09-22-core-edge-residual.pdf in the store, built by investigations/I01-.../report.py over report_lib (which gained an investigation() loader); tables by make_tables.py in data/.

title: (R35) Never compare wall time across machines: guard in query and report
description:
Decided 2026-09-22: a wall time is never compared across machines. Ratios are taken against the baseline recorded on the same machine. The machine-independent metrics, RHS evaluations and nonlinear iterations, may be compared across machines.

Why: with two machines feeding one index, a query that groups by recipe without grouping by machine silently mixes two clock speeds into one ratio.

What to do: the query tool and the campaign report refuse a wall-time ratio between rows whose machine columns differ, and say so, unless the metric is one schema.md marks machine-independent. schema.md gains a note on the machine column saying this. A test covers the refusal.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22 in the query tool: group_rows refuses a median of wall_s or ms_per_24h over rows from more than one machine, naming the machines and the fix. The report script does its ratios per campaign, and a campaign belongs to one machine. Test covers it.

title: (R35) Each machine makes its own parent runs and seeds; VM setup steps for any agent
description:
Decided 2026-09-22: no run output ever moves between machines. Each machine makes its own parent runs from scratch and cuts its own window seeds from them, and the parent's test id goes into that machine's campaign config.

Why: a parent is about a gigabyte and the seed chain must stay machine-readable within one store. The deck and grid are small and travel through the repository, so a fresh VM has everything it needs to make a parent.

What to do: write the VM setup steps as an instruction any agent can follow: clone the three repositories, build Hermes-3 at the campaign's pinned commit, make the parent run, cut the seeds, then point the runner at the campaign. Blocked by the three open portability issues, because the runner cannot start on a fresh VM until they close.
notes: 2026-09-22: seeds, grids and parent inputs now travel in the private repo hermes-solver-opt-seeds (github.com/mikekryjak/hermes-solver-opt-seeds); its README has the VM setup lines. Only dumps stay put. The round 8 candidate C2 in requirements.md should be reworded to say seeds may travel and dumps may not.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: README section 'Setting up on a new machine', general for any test, campaign and host; the three portability blockers it depended on are closed. Parent runs and seeds are made per machine, as decided.

title: (R35) One campaign belongs to one machine: name it in campaign.toml and refuse a foreign host
description:
Decided 2026-09-22: the project runs on two machines, this workstation and the user's Google VM, and each campaign belongs to exactly one of them.

Why: the runner decides which trials are settled by reading the campaign's local index, so two machines running one campaign would each repeat the other's trials. Wall time also differs between machines, and a ratio is only meaningful against a baseline measured on the same machine.

What to do: add a machine name to the [machine] table in campaign.toml. The runner compares it with the local hostname (the same value the extractor writes into the machine column) and refuses to start with a message naming both when they differ. campaign.example.toml documents the field. A test covers the refusal.

Open question: whether the name is the raw hostname or a short alias mapped in the config, since cloud hostnames change on rebuild.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: [machine] name is required in campaign.toml, check_machine() compares it with the hostname the extractor records, and Runner.run refuses with both names. Raw hostname, no alias: one name per machine, the user's choice. Test covers the refusal.

title: Repeat count per window must follow the measured nl_its spread, not a fixed three
description:
Rung 0 was sized at three repeats on the assumption that noise is machine noise of a few per cent. The overnight campaign showed wall per nonlinear iteration is within 5 per cent in 45 of 48 three-repeat cells, but nl_its varies by up to 1.8x on windows that contain the 2-6 ms transient (2.0-3.0ms, 4.0-4.1ms, 0.0-100.0ms) and by 1-3 per cent on windows that avoid it (3.0-3.2ms, 3.0-4.0ms). The ladder's noise_bound values (0.15, 0.10, 0.05) are met on the second group and missed on the first.

Decide: either move the rung-0 screening windows off the transient entirely, or size repeats per window from the measured nl_its spread, or make the runner read nl_its spread and add repeats until the ratio's range is decisive. Depends on the non-determinism issue: if the source is found and removed, the question goes away.
notes:
Study 3 buys the data this needs: rung 0 repeats go from 3 to 5, and the cliff
window test4_2.0-3.0ms becomes a noise rung at 10. Ten draws on the noisiest
window and five on the two quiet ones give a measured spread per window to size
the repeat count from, instead of one number for the whole campaign.
2026-09-23, the user: we are doing too many repeats. To discuss alongside the noise redesign (so-bwpm).
RULED 2026-09-23 by the user: limit repeats to two runs per cell for now. MUMPS determinism is attacked separately (I02, so-mzy). Context given to the user: in test4-jacobian 705 of 918 runs (77 per cent) and about 70 per cent of 61 slot-hours were repeats; machine noise is small, the spread is MUMPS round-off steering the 2.5-6 ms path.

title: (R22) The run skill tells agents to validate with a command the guard blocks
description:
The solver-opt-run skill's first campaign rule says to run run_campaign.py --dry-run before queueing a campaign, because it checks every override against the search space. The launch guard blocks that command, so the rule cannot be followed as written. Validation has to go through the library instead: load_campaign, then load_space against the campaign's search_space, then load_study for each study file, which raises on an unknown knob, a bad choice or an out-of-range value.

Either make the guard allow --dry-run, or rewrite the rule to name the library route. Noted 2026-09-21 while validating the overnight studies.

Related: check_overrides does not read the search space's depends field, so this validation does not catch a dependency violation whichever route is used.
close_reason: Duplicate of so-uk0, which already covers the blocked --dry-run. The skill-rule consequence is now recorded in that issue's notes.

title: (R17) index.tsv has no lock and three slots write it
description:
index.py reads, modifies and rewrites index.tsv through a temp file and os.replace with no lock, while three slot processes write to the same file for a whole night. Expected loss is of order one row per night at about 350 writes. A lost planned row makes that run's extraction land as unplanned with recipe, varied and slot blank, and baseline_wall then reads a blank varied as a baseline, which moves the kill cutoff for that window.

Fix: an flock around the read-modify-write in index.py.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: index.lock_index/unlock_index (flock on index.tsv.lock) around the runner's two read-modify-writes and the extractor's one. A test runs 12 writer processes and loses no row.

title: physics_diffs never computes: the seed's parent lives in the top-level index, not the campaign's
description:
Every run in the test4-jacobian campaign warns "physics_diffs not computed: no recorded run has the seed's run_id", so the check that no physics setting drifted from the parent never runs.

The cause is the campaign index split. extract.py's _seed_input searches the rows it was given for a run whose run_id matches the case's seed. It is given the CAMPAIGN's index, at campaigns/<name>/index.tsv. The seed's parent, test4_0.0-100.0ms, has a row only in the top-level index.tsv, because campaign results stay local and the parent belongs to the shared record. The two never meet, so the lookup always fails.

This is separate from the verdict column, which is a deliberate stub: _correctness_ok says in its own docstring that no reference run is chosen for any row because the rule is not settled, and design.md carries that as an open question. Nothing here asks for that rule to be decided.

What physics_diffs would catch is narrower and worth having: a run whose solver knob moved AND whose physics options moved, which would make its timing meaningless. Right now that would pass unnoticed.

Fix: let the extractor look for the seed's parent in the top-level index as well as the campaign's own, since a parent is by definition recorded there.

Found 2026-09-21, on every row of the first two studies.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-09-21: _seed_input now falls back to the top-level index when the campaign's own has no row for the seed, via _project_index. The bundle was never the problem - st.bundle_path resolves from the data directory - only finding the parent's row.

title: (R35) Dependency pinning: the requirement says pinned, pyproject deliberately does not
description:
R35 and design.md section 12 both say Python dependencies are pinned in the tool repository. pyproject.toml deliberately does the opposite, and says so: "No upper pins: this installs alongside an existing scientific Python stack, where a tight pin would force a downgrade of somebody else's numpy or pandas."

Both positions are defensible. They cannot both be the rule. On this workstation the unpinned choice is right, because the Spack environment owns numpy and pandas. On a fresh VM building from scratch, the pinned choice is what makes a run reproducible.

Decide which R35 means, and make the file and the requirement agree. If the answer is "unpinned here, pinned on the VM", that is a lock file or a constraints file, not a change to dependencies.

Raised 2026-09-21 while checking what a Google agent on the VM would need.
close_reason: Decided by the user 2026-09-22: relaxed. Dependencies stay unpinned in pyproject; no constraints file. R35's "pinned dependencies" should be amended to match; candidate to follow.

title: (R35) pyproject gives console scripts for five tools but not run_campaign
description:
pyproject.toml gives console scripts for five tools: extract-test, query-store, verify-store, add-views and can-delete. It gives none for run_campaign.py, which is the one command the whole system exists to run.

The packaging itself is sound: package-dir maps solveropt_cli to cli/, so an install works. The gap is only the missing entry point.

This matters for R35. On a fresh VM the expected route is clone, pip install, run. That route gives an agent every secondary tool and not the runner, so it has to discover that this one tool is invoked by its file path instead. Add run-campaign to [project.scripts].

Found 2026-09-21 while preparing the test4-jacobian launch.
close_reason: Done 2026-09-22: run-campaign added to [project.scripts].

title: The launch guard blocks run_campaign.py --dry-run and --status, which never launch
description:
The run-case launch guard refuses any command containing run_campaign.py run through an interpreter, including its two read-only modes: --status, which only reads the index, and --dry-run, which exists precisely so a study can be checked without launching. The guard matches on text, so it cannot tell them apart from a real launch.

Found 2026-09-21 while validating the test4-jacobian campaign. The workaround was a short script calling load_campaign and load_study directly, which proves the files but duplicates what --dry-run already does.

This matters because --dry-run is the cheap check the design puts in front of every campaign, and an agent that cannot run it will either skip the check or reimplement it each time.

Options: have the guard allow the command when --status or --dry-run is present; or split the read-only modes into their own tool that never launches, which is the more honest fix since the guard's rule then stays simple.

title: The search space omits whole families of PETSc options, and the whitelist makes them unreachable
description:
search-space.toml has 62 knobs, 12 of them on the petsc side. check_overrides refuses any knob the file does not name, so whatever is missing is unreachable: the file is a whitelist, not a starting point.

Checked against the installed PETSc 3.23.7 library, so every name below exists. Families that are absent and that bear on knobs already marked candidate:

- The line search's own settings. 16 options exist (-snes_linesearch_order, _damping, _maxstep, _minlambda, _max_it, _atol, _rtol, _ltol, _alpha and more). solver:line_search_type is a candidate, but proposing bt without its order and damping is half a knob. petsc:snes_linesearch_type is not a knob either, though the baseline recipe sets it.
- The linear-solve tolerance. BOUT++ passes PETSC_DEFAULT for KSP rtol, atol and divtol and sets only maxl (snes.cxx around line 719), so the linear tolerance sits at PETSc's default 1e-5 and nothing in the space can move it: -ksp_rtol, -ksp_atol, -ksp_divtol, -ksp_pc_side, -ksp_norm_type. Also -snes_ksp_ew, the Eisenstat-Walker adaptive forcing term, which is the standard way to stop over-solving early Newton steps. This matters little under an exact LU and a great deal under ilu, asm or hypre, all of which are allowed values of solver:pc_type.
- Matrix-free differencing. solver:matrix_free is a candidate, but the differencing parameters that decide whether it works at all are absent: -mat_mffd_type, -mat_mffd_err, -mat_mffd_umin, -mat_mffd_compute_normu, -mat_mffd_period, and the 9 -snes_mf_* options.
- Coloured finite-difference Jacobian. -mat_coloring_type and 7 more, plus -mat_fd_coloring_err, _umin, _brows, _bcols. This is the Jacobian that lag_jacobian re-uses, so its accuracy and its cost are part of every campaign already planned.
- Preconditioner robustness and reuse. -pc_factor_shift_type and -pc_factor_shift_amount for zero pivots, -pc_factor_reuse_ordering and -pc_factor_reuse_fill, which change what a refactorisation costs. Also -pc_asm_overlap, -pc_asm_type, -pc_bjacobi_blocks, without which proposing pc_type = asm or bjacobi is under-specified, and the 126 -pc_hypre_* options behind the single solver:pc_hypre_type choice.
- MUMPS. The library exposes 40 -mat_mumps_* options; the space has 6. Notably -mat_mumps_icntl_36 completes the BLR set with the icntl_35 and cntl_7 entries that are already there.

Not a request to add all of these. The point is that the file was written from one -snes_view of one configuration, and it covers that configuration's objects. Deciding which of these to admit is the user's, and each admitted knob needs the same cost note as the rest.
notes:
Measured 2026-09-21 against the full inventory (snes-space.tsv, option-space.md). The SNES path exposes 865 tuning knobs across 850 names; this file describes 85. Of the 327 that are live in the configuration the campaigns actually run, it describes 66, so it covers a fifth of what is reachable without changing a single type choice. That is scope, not a fault, but it should be stated rather than assumed.

The preconditioner families added earlier close part of the gap. What is still missing and still unreachable: the line search's own options beyond its type, the linear-solve tolerance including -snes_ksp_ew, the matrix-free differencing parameters, and the coloured Jacobian knobs. The line search matters first, and the user has said it becomes reachable as soon as the preconditioner stops being an effectively direct solver.

title: Measure what share of the residual norm the scaling floor carries
description:
The scale_vars floor is reached in nearly every run - fourteen of sixteen runs report a minimum scaling factor of exactly rtol. That proves the floor activates. It does not prove the floored elements matter.

A handful of elements out of 5600 could contribute nothing to the residual norm, or could dominate it. Which one is true decides whether any residual-based objective is usable before the code defect is fixed, and that objective is on the roadmap for pseudo-transient methods.

This needs no new runs. The residual data is already stored: resid_final, resid_drop and resid_per_rhs in the index, and resid_regions.tsv in every bundle.

What to produce: for one or two runs, the fraction of the squared residual norm contributed by elements whose scaling factor sits at the floor, and which variables those elements belong to. The expectation is that they are momenta near stagnation points, since densities and temperatures are floored positive by the physics and stay clear of rtol.

Follow the postprocess skill. If the stored per-region data cannot separate floored elements, say so and state what capture would be needed, rather than approximating.
notes: 2026-09-22 partial answer from the 100 ms runs' dumps (details in the Investigation 01 issue notes): the dump resid_* fields are the scaled residual, and while the neutral density at the core edge sits within a factor of a few of the rtol scaling floor (2-10 ms) the neutral equations hold the whole norm in those cells; once it climbs a hundred times above the floor the neutral share is zero and Pe holds the norm. This is consistent with the floor carrying most of the norm through the transient, but it is a correlation in time, not a measurement of the floored elements' share; that still needs the per-element scale factors.

title: scale_vars floors zero-valued elements at rtol, amplifying their residual by 1/rtol
description:
THE DEFECT. BOUT-dev src/solver/impls/snes/snes.cxx:627-635 computes the per-element scale factor as

    norm    = max(|x_i|, rtol / scale_i)      // scale_i starts at 1
    x_i    /= norm
    scale_i = norm

and the residual is then divided by that scale (snes.cxx:1494, VecPointwiseDivide(f, f, var_scaling_factors)). Any element whose value is exactly zero therefore takes scale = rtol, and its residual is amplified by 1/rtol = 1e5 at the default tolerances. Those elements then dominate the residual norm and the convergence test, and the solver is effectively asked to converge empty cells to an absolute tolerance of about atol*rtol.

PROVEN, not inferred. Same case (test4scratch), same state, only rtol changed:

    scale_vars off, rtol 1e-6    initial residual         26.9651
    scale_vars on,  rtol 1e-6    initial residual 19,360,394.5437594
    scale_vars on,  rtol 1e-5    initial residual  1,936,039.4543759

The two scaled residuals are in the ratio 10.000000 — exactly 1/rtol. That can only happen if the norm is dominated by floored elements.

WHY IT MATTERS. It makes scale_vars unusable from scratch in some configurations, which is not a reasonable thing to ask users to work around. Observed consequences:
  - VanAlbada builds from scratch with scale_vars FAIL at the first step (SNES reason -9, DIVERGED_DTOL, then -5). MC builds from scratch survive the identical scaling and identical initial residual. Record: perftests/test4dev/test4scratch-2026-07-2{6,7,9}-* , three directories suffixed -fail, plus 07-29-master-mc-mumps2 which completes.
  - It killed four ST40 high-resolution runs on 2026-08-25 (fluxlim/st40-flim/st40fl9a-d, all void). Diagnosis in separate-neutral-fluxlim/implementation_log.md, 2026-08-25.

THE STRUCTURAL PART NO INPUT CAN FIX. Momentum fields (NVd, NVd+) are exactly zero at t=0 in every cold start, and correctly so. So a from-scratch run always has floored elements and always reports 'Var scaling: 1e-05 -> ...'. Setting non-zero initial densities and pressures removed the FATAL cases (those were the zero fields carrying explosive ionisation/recycling sources, ddt(Pd) reaching 1e17) but did not remove the floor itself.

PROPOSED FIX. Floor the scale per FIELD rather than per element at rtol — e.g. max(|x_i|, floor_frac * max|x| over that field), so an empty cell inherits the scale of the field it belongs to instead of a pathological one. Roughly five lines in snes.cxx. Alternatives worth weighing: expose the floor as its own option instead of reusing rtol (rtol is a convergence tolerance and has no business setting a variable scale); or exclude floored elements from the convergence norm.

NOTE the code's own density_floor (1e-8 normalised) is a thousand times BELOW the rtol floor, so it offers no protection.

ALSO TO FIX HERE: finding F18 in findings.md presents the mumps1->mumps2 ladder (13.8x) without saying it was measured entirely on RESTARTS (test4steady/test5steady logs say 'Restarting from ID: ...') and without naming the slope limiter. As written the ladder reads as portable to a from-scratch VanAlbada run, where it fails. F18 needs both caveats.
notes:
2026-09-20 measurement, from logs already on disk. The floor is reached in nearly every run, not rarely. When diagnose is on the solver prints its smallest scaling factor per rescale. Across sixteen runs carrying that line, fourteen report exactly 1e-5, which is rtol. That is the fingerprint of the floor: a scaling factor landing precisely on rtol cannot be a genuine variable magnitude. Confirmation from a run that used a different tolerance: test5steady-2026-08-01-va-step3-tolerance reports exactly 1e-6, its own rtol. The two runs that escaped are test2_20.0-21.0ms-2026-09-19 at 5.25e-5 and test5steady-2026-08-01-va-step4-matrixfree at 4.69e-6, both short.

Two corrections to how this issue has been described. The trigger is not a variable of exactly zero. It is any element whose normalised magnitude falls below rtol, and exact zero is only the extreme case. And the non-zero neutral initial conditions do not remove the exposure: densities and temperatures are floored positive by the physics and stay clear of 1e-5, but momenta are signed, pass through zero at every stagnation point, and nothing floors them.

Still unmeasured: what share of the residual norm the floored elements actually carry. The diagnostic proves the floor activates, not that it dominates. See the follow-up issue.

title: Line-search tuning is the next lever on test5, not the Jacobian
description:
Where the CVODE-like scan leaves test5steady, and what to attack next.

Best configuration is target_its=5 plus snes_linesearch_type=bt on SNES-MUMPS-2: 208 s against a 676 s baseline and 1249 s for CVODE-2. Physics unchanged to 0.002%.

Jacobian construction is still 80% of that run, but it CANNOT be reduced by lagging. Measured sweep on the best configuration, assembled operator:

  lag   wall    ncalls   nl_its  fails   jac   t_jac
   3    208 s   133986    1204     96    803   0.805
   5    212 s   135812    1249    154    789   0.779
  10    241 s   154348    1154    243    866   0.756

Raising the lag does not reduce builds. It raises FAILURES - 96 to 154 to 243 - because a staler Jacobian gives worse Newton steps, and every failure calls SNESSetLagJacobian(snes, 1) (snes.cxx:857), restored only after a success, so the whole cascade rebuilds per iteration. The scheduled saving and the failure-driven cost cancel, and past lag 5 the failures win.

General principle worth carrying to other tests: lag_jacobian pays only where the solve is nearly failure-free. F18 got -58% from lag 1 to 3 on test4steady with an identical trajectory - and test4steady at that point had one failure. Where failures are common the lever is self-defeating.

So builds are failure-dominated, and the remaining 96 failures are the target. Their character has changed since the scan began: at the baseline they were 56% DTOL divergence and 44% max-iterations; at the best configuration they are 79% line-search failures (-6) and 21% max-iterations. The solver is no longer blowing up - it is failing to find an acceptable step length.

That makes line-search tuning the next scan, and it is completely untouched: the alternative types (l2, cp, basic with damping), the damping parameter, maxstep, and whether the line search should be allowed more function evaluations. Each is a one-line change on a 208 s test.
acceptance_criteria: A line-search scan on test5steady from the 208 s configuration, reporting failure count by reason and wall clock per variant.

title: test5 count scatter looks ~10x worse than test4's, and the scan depends on it
description:
The CVODE-like scan's baseline repeat came out 11% above the 2026-07-30 row on work counts, with only diagnose_failures intentionally different between them:

                          wall   ncalls   nl_its  fails  jac builds  concurrency
  2026-07-30 va-mumps2    638 s  385102     913    661     2406         2.09
  2026-08-01 baseline     676 s  438333    1007    731     2739         1.00

Physics is identical - peak target Te agrees to 0.003% - so this is the same answer reached by 11% more work.

Two explanations and one run cannot separate them:
- diagnose_failures perturbs the trajectory. It should not: it only takes min/max reductions over fields on failure. But it does add roughly 10k collective reductions, and F16's mechanism for non-determinism is precisely that reductions are not bitwise reproducible and convergence tests near threshold then tip differently.
- test5's count scatter is genuinely much larger than test4's. F16 measured 1.8% on test4steady. test5 has 731 failures, each one a decision near a threshold, so the failure count is itself the thing scattering and it amplifies.

Either way this matters immediately: F16's 1.8% figure is a test4 number and must not be used to judge test5 differences. If the true scatter here is ~10%, then any step in the scan worth under about 15% is unproven from one run each.

The scan itself is unaffected - every step is compared against this baseline under identical conditions, which is why the repeat was included.

Cheapest resolution: one more repeat of the baseline configuration. If it lands near 438k the option is innocent and the scatter is real; if it lands near 385k, diagnose_failures is the cause.
acceptance_criteria: A second baseline repeat, and a stated count-scatter figure for test5steady that the scan's conclusions are read against.

title: A crawling rung must record a progress rate, not a hole
description:
Six rungs have now aborted on the 2 h no-output cap. Each carries nl_its and solver_fails but no wall_s, no sim_time_ms, no ncalls and no ms_per_24h, so each is a hole in the history rather than a data point.

It does not have to be. Every aborted run ran for a known wall duration and reached a known simulated time - a35e2f5e got to 0.350 of 20 ms in two hours - and ms_per_24h is already a column in the index. Filling it on the abort path converts the six existing holes into six comparable measurements, and they are already comparable to the completed rungs because that column is what the completed ones report too.

This was a nuisance for a retrospective ladder. For the standing watch it is close to fatal: the regressions most worth catching are the ones that make a run too slow to finish, so they will abort rather than return a slow number. An abort that records nothing says only that something happened.

Scope: the abort path in the run tooling and the extractor, so that outcome=crawl_aborted still fills wall_s, sim_time_ms and ms_per_24h from what the run achieved before it was killed. Backfill the six existing rows from their logs.

Related but distinct from so-oze, which is about a build that never ran.
acceptance_criteria: The six existing crawl_aborted rows carry a progress rate, and a newly aborted rung fills it without hand editing.

title: Cap kappa_par_e as a diagnostic: is the dt ceiling conduction-set?
description:
Establishes whether the flash is what sets the maximum stable step on test5, as opposed to being a passenger.

Two knobs, both available now:
- e:conduction_kappa_max, already implemented in Hermes-3 from the cf project. Harmonic cap applied after the physical limiter: kappa_eff = kappa * kappa_max / (kappa + kappa_max). Smooth, so it does not introduce a residual kink.
- e:kappa_limit_alpha = 0.2, matching both test4s. test5 currently runs with the limiter OFF (-1), so kappa_par is uncapped Spitzer at 119-288 eV and around 1e18 m-3.

Both CHANGE THE PHYSICS. They are diagnostics for the ceiling question, not entries in the speed table, and any result must be reported that way.

Prediction if the conduction reading is right: the failure count collapses and the accepted timestep rises by roughly the factor kappa is reduced by. If the failures survive an aggressive cap, the ceiling is set by something else and this whole epic needs rethinking.

Worth knowing independently of the solver: an unlimited Spitzer parallel heat flux at these conditions may be exceeding the free-streaming limit, which would be a physics problem in the test case itself.
acceptance_criteria: test5steady at two or more kappa caps, reporting failure count, median and peak accepted timestep, and the physics drift against the uncapped baseline.

title: Line search: basic to bt on the MUMPS recipes
description:
Both MUMPS recipes set petsc:snes_linesearch_type = basic - a full undamped Newton step with no backtracking. When the controller demands 2.9x and the step is too long, nothing inside the solve can recover; it can only fail and be rejected.

PETSc default bt would cut the step back and converge instead. This is the part that converts a controller overshoot into a hard failure, and it is one line.

Expect it to interact with so-yjs.2 and with the tolerance issue: all three reduce failures by different routes. Order matters for attribution, so run it on its own.

Note the flash reading: if the failures are localised over-long steps into the flash cells, a line search is exactly the right remedy and does not change the answer. diagnose_failures would say so directly.
acceptance_criteria: test5steady with snes_linesearch_type = bt, failure count and wall against the SNES-MUMPS-2 row, physics unchanged.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01 on test5steady, as step 2 of the CVODE-like scan, on top of target_its = 5. snes_linesearch_type basic -> bt, everything else held:

                     wall    ncalls   nl_its  fails  jac builds
  + target_its 5     432 s   279790    1210    311     1748
  + linesearch bt    208 s   133986    1204     96      803
                     -52%     -52%      -0%   -69%     -54%

Physics unchanged: peak target Te 131.0486 against the baseline's 131.0465, 0.0016%.

The failure profile confirms the mechanism exactly, and this is the cleanest causal evidence in the project so far:

  reason              baseline   +target_its   +bt
  -9  DTOL              412         151          0
  -5  MAX_IT            319         160         21
  -6  LINE_SEARCH         0           0         75

Every DTOL divergence is gone. Those were undamped full Newton steps blowing the residual up by four orders of magnitude; with a line search the same events now appear as 75 line-search failures, meaning the solver looked for a shorter step and reported when it could not find one, instead of taking the long one and diverging.

Nonlinear iterations are flat at ~1204 while failures fell 69% and Jacobian builds 54%. Same Newton work, far less of it wasted.

Cumulative with step 1: 676 s -> 208 s, 3.25x, from two one-line settings. SNES is now 6.0x faster than CVODE-2 on this test in wall clock and 6.1x in RHS evaluations - the test where SNES was believed to lose.

Still to attack: t_jac_frac is 0.805, so building the Jacobian is still 80% of the run and the matrix-free step is where the remaining headroom is.

title: Tighten atol on test5, separately from the controller
description:
atol = 1e-3 on the MUMPS-2 recipe is doing three things at once on test5, and all three hurt:

1. It lets the Te corrugations grow. Measured controlled on test4steady across the tolerance step of the MUMPS-1 to MUMPS-2 scan (atol 1e-7 to 1e-3, rtol 1e-6 to 1e-5, same case, same build): max|ddt(Pe)| median 2.57e6 to 9.11e7 (35x), rms 2.09e5 to 3.37e6 (16x), max/rms 12.5 to 22.8. Peak dt is nearly identical between the two runs (4.54e4 against 4.87e4) so the step-interpolation artefact cannot account for it.
2. It hollows out each solve. 354 of 470 accepted steps on test5steady converge in ONE Newton iteration.
3. Through (2) it pins the timestep controller at its maximum. facP = (100/nl_its)^0.233, so nl_its=1 gives 2.92, and the controller demands that growth after three quarters of the steps.

The same tolerance loosening was measured as a 46 percent saving on test4steady (F18), on a case with the flux limiter on and 1300x less conduction stiffness. Carrying it to test5 imports all three effects into the one case that cannot absorb them.

Run this SEPARATELY from the target_its change (so-yjs.2). Both calm the controller; only the tolerance touches the fluctuations. Running them together confounds the controller-overshoot term with the fluctuation-driven Newton-radius term, and telling those apart is the whole question.
acceptance_criteria: test5steady at tightened atol, reported against so-yjs.2 run at loose atol, with failure count, Jacobian builds, nl_its distribution and max|ddt(Pe)| for each.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01 on test5steady as step 3 of the CVODE-like scan, and it is a decisive NEGATIVE. atol 1e-3 -> 1e-7, rtol 1e-5 -> 1e-6, on top of target_its=5 and linesearch bt:

                     wall     ncalls   nl_its  fails  jac builds  accepted steps
  + linesearch bt     208 s   133986    1204     96      803        ~700
  + tight tolerance  2071 s  1359841   10408    954     8148        3695
                     +896%    +915%    +764%

Ten times slower. Whatever fluctuation benefit F28 predicts is swamped by an order of magnitude of extra solver work, so tightening tolerance is wrong on test5 on cost grounds. Do not carry this into a recipe.

The mechanism is the coupling this issue was warned about, and it runs the unhelpful way. Tightening lifts nl_its off 1 - the distribution moves from 'almost always 1' to a spread with mode 2 and a long tail - and the controller reads nl_its: facP = (target_its/nl_its)^0.233. At target_its=5, nl_its=1 grows dt by 1.44 per success; nl_its=2 grows it by 1.23 and nl_its=3 by 1.13. So tightening the tolerance SLOWS dt growth, dt stays small, and the run needs 3695 accepted steps instead of about 700 - while each of those steps also costs several times more Newton iterations.

Design consequence, and it generalises beyond this run: target_its cannot be chosen independently of the tolerance, because the tolerance sets the nl_its the controller reads. target_its should sit just above the typical nl_its that the tolerance produces, which is the only way the controller becomes genuinely two-way. At this tolerance the right target would be about 2-3, not 5. Nobody has tested that pairing.

This also poisons step 4 of the ladder, which inherits the tolerance. A branch run (test5steady-2026-08-01-va-step3b-matrixfree) puts matrix-free on step 2 instead.

title: A 1D perftest for history, based on 1D-recycling-dthe
description:
The 2D test cannot measure most of the window. test2_0-20ms completed on only 5 of 12 anchors: everything from the 2026-01 anchor backwards collapses its timestep to ~5e-5 inside the first output interval and is aborted. So the ladder measures five months of a twelve-month history, and the older half is unmeasurable rather than slow.

The user's proposal, 2026-08-01: build the history test on hermes-3's tests/integrated/1D-recycling instead. Its component list is d+, d, e, sheath_boundary, collisions, recycling, reactions, electron_force_balance, neutral_parallel_diffusion - about as complete as 1D allows - it runs fast, and it is far more stable than 2D. Stability is the point: a test that only runs on the recent half of the window cannot answer how performance evolved across it.

Convenient side effect: the migration ledger was verified against this very input, so the option translations already have evidence behind them.

Open before this can be specified:
- Sizing. How much simulated time, and nout, to be long enough to time reliably but cheap enough to run twelve times over.
- Start mode. From scratch, or from a seed like the 2D tests use.
- Recipe. SNES-MUMPS-1 for continuity with the 2D ladder, or something suited to 1D.
- Whether the MC limiter constraint still binds, and whether a 1D case is sensitive to the limiter at all.
- Whether the older anchors need input migrations beyond the ones already in the ledger.

Not urgent - the user has parked it.
acceptance_criteria: A named test definition and sizing that runs on all twelve anchors, or a recorded reason why some still cannot.

UNPARKED and raised to P1 on 2026-08-01. The user extended perf-bisect from a one-off backward ladder to a standing watch that gains a rung as each PR lands on master. That makes this case a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have, for two independent reasons:

- Cost. A 2D rung is 40-45 min when it completes, which does not work at merge cadence. A 1D case does.
- Coverage. Everything from the 2026-01 anchor backwards collapses its timestep and aborts, so the 2D ladder can only ever measure five months of the twelve-month window.

The five open questions in the description - sizing, start mode, recipe, whether the MC constraint binds, whether older anchors need further migrations - are now blocking rather than deferred. Answer them first.

Limitation to record while building it: a 1D watch has no perpendicular transport, no topology and no X-point, so it cannot see the flashes or the NVd corrugation. It catches broad regressions cheaply and misses the 2D-specific ones entirely. So it is the per-merge watch, and the 2D case is retained at low cadence - epoch boundaries, or when the 1D watch flags something - rather than being replaced by it.

title: Make hcompile.sh parameterised enough to drive from a script
description:
perf-bisect cannot drive builds until this is fixed, and the fix is worth having regardless. Read of /home/mike/work/hcompile.sh (170 lines) as of 2026-07-31:

Blockers for automation
- BUILD_DIR, LIMITER, CONDMETHOD and HERMES_DIR are hardcoded top-of-file variables edited by hand, above a graveyard of ~15 commented-out alternatives. These are exactly the four things perf-bisect must vary per invocation, and none has a flag.
- PETSC_DIR is hardcoded to /home/mike/work/petsc-3.23.3. That pins PETSc for every build and is the variable the feasibility probe may need to move.
- cmake --build -j 32 is hardcoded. A 32-way build overlapping a timed run corrupts the timing; the job count must be settable. perf-bisect is serial so it cannot self-collide, but it can collide with a solver-opt run in another slot.
- No set -e. A failed cmake configure falls through to cmake --build, so the script can report the build's status for a configure that never succeeded. Automation needs an unambiguous pass/fail.
- cd $HERMES_DIR is relative, so the script only works when run from /home/mike/work.
- Nothing records what was built - no commit sha captured anywhere.

Bug found while reading, independent of perf-bisect
- The -e guard rejects any configure-affecting option and tests CHECK_LEVEL != 0, but CHECK_LEVEL defaults to 2 and -d sets it to 4. So -e can never pass its own guard: express mode always exits 2. The guard should compare against the defaults it actually has (2 and RelWithDebInfo), not 0.

Recommended scope: do NOT rewrite. Turn the four hardcoded variables into flags whose defaults are today's values, add set -e, and make -j settable. Every existing invocation then behaves byte-identically. The script is shared with the physics-build campaigns and a redesign risks silently changing builds those campaigns depend on.

Open question: whether the -e guard bug should be fixed in the same change or separately, since fixing it makes a currently-dead code path live.
notes:
Rewritten 2026-07-31, tested with a stub cmake against a throwaway repo; awaiting the user's review of the diff before closing. Original kept at /home/mike/work/hcompile.sh.orig (that directory is not a git repo, so there was no other undo).

Done:
- BUILD_NAME (-b), LIMITER (-s), CONDMETHOD (-m), HERMES_DIR (-r), PETSC_DIR (-P), jobs (-j), CHECK (-k) are now flags. Defaults reproduce the previous hardcoded values exactly, so a bare invocation builds what it built before.
- Build directory is composed, not given: build-<va|mc>-<name>. Two builds differing only by slope limiter can no longer overwrite each other.
- set -e and set -o pipefail, so a failed configure no longer falls through to the build step.
- Relative -r resolves against the script's own directory, so it runs from any cwd.
- Settings validated up front (limiter, conduction method, numeric CHECK and jobs, repo exists) rather than failing inside CMake.
- Prints the commit sha and branch it is building, plus the full configuration.
- The commented-out BUILD_DIR graveyard is gone; those names survive in the .orig backup.

The -e guard bug was fixed in the same change, contrary to the open question, because making CHECK a flag removed the option of leaving it: the old guard inferred 'user passed a configure option' by comparing CHECK_LEVEL against 0, which cannot work once any value is settable. It now tracks which configure-affecting flags were actually parsed. Express mode works for the first time; -b, -s, -r and -j are permitted with it since they only locate the build or control the build step.

Not done, deliberately: only the slope limiter is baked into the name, as asked. Conduction method is not, so build-va-master built with Harmonic still silently overwrites build-va-master built with Original.

Follow-up 2026-07-31, all tested with a stub cmake and a real pty:
- Confirmation summary in sdrun.py's style (orange box rule, dim labels, yellow git info, green flags), showing repo, commit, physics options, build type, PETSc dir, jobs, mode and extra flags, then Proceed? [y/N].
- -y skips the prompt. Required when stdout/stdin is not a terminal: without it a non-interactive call aborts rather than building unattended. This is what lets perf-bisect drive the script. Stricter than sdrun.py, which accepts a piped answer.
- Conduction method now appended to the build name when it is not Original: build-va-harmonic-master, build-mc-productjk-master. Original stays out, so existing names are unchanged.
- Default job count changed from 32 to 1, at the user's request. Protects timed runs from a build stealing cores; the cost is that an interactive full build now needs an explicit -j.
- The -l build log is written to the directory the script was called from, not the repo it builds. It was already doing this by accident (the redirect preceded the cd); now it is explicit, and the redirect happens after the prompt so the summary stays on screen.
close_reason: Already satisfied: hcompile.sh takes -b name, -s limiter, -m method, -r repo, -j jobs, -S slot and -y non-interactive, which is everything run_ladder.py needs to drive it.

title: perf-bisect: a commits lookup table joining sha to date and subject
description:
index.tsv records hermes_commit as a bare sha and carries no commit date at all, so no row in the store can be read as old or new code without looking the sha up by hand. perf-bisect makes this acute (the commit is its independent variable) but the gap is not specific to it.

Recommendation: one commits table, not a second run ledger. Two files of one-row-per-run is how the two projects get confused; one run ledger plus one lookup table cannot be, because they are different shapes and join on the sha. Proposed commits.tsv in perftest-results, keyed by hermes_commit: date, subject, bout_commit, and for perf-bisect rows the anchor flag and why that commit was chosen. Every solver-opt row gets human-readable provenance for free; no date or subject is duplicated into index.tsv, where it would drift and add noise (R11).

Open question: whether extraction should append a row automatically for any commit it has not seen, or whether the table is curated by hand for anchors only.
close_reason: commits.tsv and make_commits_table.py are in notebooks/perftests/perf-bisect/, committed in 481426b. Twelve anchors joined to date, subject and the BOUT++ commit each pins. The generator rebuilds from ladder.toml and the index, so a new run's commit appears without hand editing, which also settles the issue's open question about whether extraction should append rows.

title: perf-bisect: build-run-discard automation under a hard disk budget
description:
Disk decides the loop shape: 69 GB free of 915 G (93% used) and a build dir is 3.6 GB, so 18 resident builds (65 GB) is impossible. Serial only: build one commit, run the test, extract to the store, delete the build.

Settled 2026-07-31: keep NO build directories. Not the binary either. The store is the surviving record, same bargain as R8; a commit that needs re-measuring is rebuilt from its sha, which is deterministic. Peak disk is then one build, not twelve.

Use one clone with a git worktree per commit rather than N clones: a worktree cannot be confused about which commit it is on, and costs a fraction of the disk.

Compile licence, granted by the user 2026-07-31: the standing rule is that compiling Hermes builds is the user's job, and this is the one exception. It is made safe by location - everything clone, worktree and build lives under /home/mike/work/hermes-bisect, used exclusively for perf-bisect. Nothing here ever touches /home/mike/work/hermes-3 or its 85 GB of existing builds, and the exception does not extend to any other project.
design:
Driver shape, proposed 2026-07-31.

Orchestrate, never reimplement. The driver calls hcompile.sh, reset_test.py, apply_recipe.py, sdrun.py and extract_test.py as subprocesses. Every step therefore stays runnable by hand with the same command, and there is one source of truth per operation. A driver that reimplements any of them creates a second way to build or run that drifts from the first.

State lives in index.tsv, not a private state file. The driver decides what is left to do by reading the store, which is already the rule that the index defines what exists. That makes it idempotent and resumable: interrupt it, rerun it, and it picks up the anchors without rows. A private progress file would be a second record able to disagree with the index, which is the failure this project keeps designing against.

Per anchor, in order: create the worktree and update submodules recursively; build pinned to the slot; reset the test; apply the recipe and the migrations for that commit; open the index row; launch; wait; extract; delete the build, the worktree and the case directory. Each step skippable if its output already exists.

A build failure is data, not an abort. Old anchors failing to compile is the answer to the window question, so the driver records the outcome on the row and moves to the next anchor. It must never silently skip: an anchor with no row and no recorded failure is indistinguishable from one never attempted.

Everything that defines the study - the twelve anchors, the migration ledger, nout, the recipe, the slot - is read from one config file, not embedded in the code. Slot is a parameter defaulting to 1 (cores 2-11); the user confirmed slots 2 and 3 are busy now but that will change.

Lives in the perf-bisect analysis directory, not sdtools: it encodes this study's choices. The reusable pieces it calls are already in sdtools and stay there.
notes: 2026-09-20 audit: reset from in_progress to open. Claimed 2026-07-31 and nothing was built; the design above is complete but no driver exists. It was showing as the only active work in the tracker, which was misleading.

title: perf-bisect: option migration ledger for input files that changed over 12 months
description: One input file per commit drifts and hides what actually differs. Proposal: one canonical input per test plus an ordered ledger of migrations (applies-before commit/date, section, key-then, key-now, kind, note); the input for a commit is the canonical file with every later migration applied in reverse. One rename is then one row, not N file edits. Critical distinction the ledger must encode: a rename with identical behaviour (SNES-MUMPS-1 still says pid_controller while test2scratch/BOUT.inp says timestep_control = pid_nonlinear_its) gets migrated silently; a changed default or changed semantics must NOT be migrated, because that change is part of what is being measured and forcing the old value measures a configuration nobody ran. Every materialised input goes into the run bundle. Open question: where the ledger lives, given hermes-perftest is read-only.
design:
First ledger content, determined 2026-07-31.

Keying rule, and the reason the ledger cannot be a list of dates: an option's availability follows the BOUT++ commit each anchor pins, not the calendar. timestep_control replaced pid_controller in BOUT-dev on 2026-02-11 (b2102d05), but hermes-3 only picked it up at the 2026-05-15 submodule bump - three months later. A ledger keyed on anchor date would migrate three anchors wrongly. Key every row on the pinned submodule commit.

Measured across the twelve anchors:

  anchor    date        BOUT-dev    option
  a35e2f5e  2025-08-27  c4c149a28   pid_controller
  6c73a474  2025-09-17  c4c149a28   pid_controller
  a9f8f30d  2025-10-29  c4c149a28   pid_controller
  e027256d  2025-11-21  aae67a54a   pid_controller
  e0f1ebfb  2025-12-15  fc15ca8c1   pid_controller
  f6ae2d1e  2026-01-29  7d28d67c3   pid_controller
  920ba829  2026-03-01  7d28d67c3   pid_controller
  e1fe3af7  2026-03-26  7d28d67c3   pid_controller
  8220ead4  2026-04-24  7d28d67c3   pid_controller
  2eeda48f  2026-05-15  8218f71a2   timestep_control
  1084ad65  2026-06-25  c7020b4fb   timestep_control
  20581461  2026-07-17  2384555b6   timestep_control

Classification: migrate silently. It is a rename plus a type change - pid_controller was a bool defaulting to false, timestep_control is an enum - but for the value in use the mapping is exact: pid_controller = true is timestep_control = pid_nonlinear_its. Behaviour is preserved, so this is not one of the changes that must be left alone as part of what is being measured.

Convenient accident: SNES-MUMPS-1 as written already says pid_controller = true, so it applies unchanged to the first nine anchors and needs the substitution only for the last three.

This matters beyond tidiness because BOUT++ aborts on unused options: today's test2scratch/BOUT.inp names timestep_control and would abort on any of the first nine anchors.
notes:
Scope widened by the probe 2026-07-31: the ledger must cover compile-time build options, not only BOUT.inp options. The limiter is the proof - HERMES_SLOPE_LIMITER=VanAlbada is accepted by CMake at a 2025-08 commit and generates a config header naming a type BOUT++ did not yet define, so the build dies at 82% of the compile with no warning at configure time. Same class of problem as an input option that changed name or default, and worse in kind, because the failure is late and its message names a C++ type rather than the setting that caused it.

So the ledger has two sections with the same shape: input options and build options, each row saying from which commit a setting is valid and what it was before.

PARENT
  ↑ ○ so-cnv: (EPIC) perf-bisect: how Hermes-3 performance evolved across development (F5) ● P1

DEPENDS ON
  → ✓ so-wvw: perf-bisect: does the oldest anchor still build? (window feasibility) ● P1

Launched rung 1 on 2026-07-31 and it aborted at init: 'Could not find braginskii_collisions'. Three things came out of it.

title: solver_fails records the worst step, not the total
description:
extract.py line 833 sets solver_fails = snes['solver_fails'].max(), while the adjacent nl_its and lin_its use .sum(). The column therefore holds the largest failure count seen in any single output step, not the run's cumulative failures.

Found 2026-07-30 on test5steady under SNES-MUMPS-2: the index row says 7, the log says 661 across 353 reporting steps. Those 661 failures are the entire explanation for that run's cost - each one rejects a step, cuts the timestep and forces a Jacobian rebuild, which is how a 20x100 grid covering 0.5 ms burned 385102 residual evaluations and 638 s. Anyone reading the index alone sees 7 and concludes the run was healthy.

Whether .max() was deliberate is unclear - a worst-burst figure has some value, since the recipe aborts on max_snes_failures consecutive failures. But the name and the neighbouring columns both say cumulative, and the cumulative number is the one that explains cost.

Suggest recording both: solver_fails as the sum, and a separate worst-burst column if the abort margin is worth tracking.
acceptance_criteria: The index carries the cumulative failure count for a run. If a worst-burst figure is also wanted it occupies its own named column. Existing SNES rows are re-extracted so the column means the same thing throughout.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-07-31. extract.py now records solver_fails as the sum, matching nl_its and lin_its, and the per-step worst moves to a new solver_fails_max column. Both documented in schema.md. All 13 affected rows recomputed from their stored bundles rather than re-extracted, since several case directories are already deleted: test5steady MUMPS-2 now reads 661 where it read 7, test5stiff 245 where it read 5. 20 extractor tests pass.

The correction changed a conclusion: test4 is not failure-free, its MUMPS-1 baselines fail 24 and 43 times. What is failure-free is MUMPS-2 on test4, and the run that removes them is scale_vars - across study 1's scan the count goes 24, 24, 23, 0 as it is switched on. On test5 that stops working, which sharpens the open question.

title: Recipes are stale against current BOUT++ and abort on startup
description:
Two recipes in the read-only hermes-perftest repo set options that current BOUT++ rejects. Both abort the run at startup, so they cost a full setup-and-launch cycle each time.

SNES-MUMPS-1 sets solver:pid_controller = true. Nothing reads it - renamed to timestep_control, whose default pid_nonlinear_its is the same behaviour - and the perftest inputs set error_on_unused_options = true, so the run aborts. Hit twice: study 1 on test4steady, and again setting up test4stiff.

CVODE-2 sets solver:use_precon = True. Current BOUT++ throws on it outright, pointing at cvode_precon_method. The replacement is NOT the default: cvode_precon_method defaults to none, and the auto value falls through to the petsc preconditioner whenever the model registers none of its own. The faithful equivalent of the old use_precon=true is cvode_precon_method = user, set explicitly. Getting this wrong silently changes which preconditioner CVODE uses, which is the whole subject of the CVODE-beats-SNES puzzle.

Both were fixed by hand in the case BOUT.inp, so the deviation lands in the diffs column of every affected row and has to be justified in varied each time.

This also explains part of the epoch problem: the June baselines were run on a BOUT++ that accepted these options. A recipe that no longer applies cleanly is a signal that the code moved underneath the baseline.

The recipes live in hermes-perftest, read-only for this project, so the fix is not ours to make directly. Options: ask for a commit there, or carry patched copies and record which file was used.
acceptance_criteria: Applying SNES-MUMPS-1 or CVODE-2 to a fresh case produces an input that runs without a hand edit, or the project has an agreed patched-recipe path and the index records which recipe file was used. The CVODE preconditioner choice is recorded explicitly, not left to auto.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-07-31 in apply_recipe.py, which now translates retired options as it applies a recipe and says loudly what it did and why. Covers solver:pid_controller -> timestep_control = pid_nonlinear_its, and solver:use_precon -> cvode_precon_method = user or none by value.

The translation table is deliberately faithfulness-first: an entry must reproduce exactly what the retired option did. A known-retired option carrying an unrecognised value exits with an error rather than guessing, because a wrong translation silently changes what a recipe means and is worse than the abort it prevents. cvode_precon_method is the reason for that rule - its default (none) and its auto value both differ from what use_precon = true meant.

Each rewritten line carries a comment naming the option it replaced, and the tool prints a reminder that the case now differs from its named recipe. Verified on both stale recipes and on SNES-MUMPS-2, which passes through silently. The read-only recipe files were not touched.

title: Option diff reports derived defaults as changes
description:
Study 1's option diff lists solver:pseudo_alpha and solver:pseudo_alpha_minimum as differing between the MUMPS-1 and MUMPS-2 runs. Nobody set either. Their defaults are derived - pseudo_alpha = 100 * atol * solver:timestep, and the minimum is 0.1 * pseudo_alpha - so relaxing atol from 1e-7 to 1e-3 moved them four decades as a consequence. The diff reports one real change three times.

They are also inert: every run uses equation_form = rearranged_backward_euler, so the pseudo-transient path never executes and pseudo_alpha is never read. They appear in options_used because BOUT++'s SNES solver queries all its options in the constructor's member-initialiser list, before the equation form is known, so an option belonging to a dead code path still records as consulted. param_diff cannot tell that apart from a live setting.

This recurs on every tolerance change and on any other derived default, so it is noise the reader has to learn to ignore - against R11.

Proposed fix: BOUT.settings records 'source: default' per option and the log prints '(default)'. Split the diff on that. Options sourced from an input file are deliberate and stay in the main list; options sourced from a default moved as a consequence and go in a separate collapsed group. General, needs no hand-maintained list of inert options.

Open question: whether a default-sourced difference is ever worth surfacing on its own - it would be, if two runs used different builds whose defaults differ. Within one build it always traces back to an input that the diff already shows.
acceptance_criteria: Option diff separates input-sourced differences from default-sourced ones; the MUMPS-1 to MUMPS-2 diff shows atol and rtol as the change, with pseudo_alpha listed as derived rather than as a peer.
close_reason:
Fixed 2026-07-31. The log line parser already captured each option's origin marker - 'default', 'user_default', or the input path - and discarded it. Now threaded through options_used(with_defaulted=True) into diff_option_sets, which splits off a derived group: keys that differ but that EVERY case took from a code default. If any case set one deliberately it stays in the main list. The cover names them in one line instead of tabulating them as peers.

On the MUMPS-1 to MUMPS-2 diff the main list is now the five deliberate changes (atol, rtol, lag_jacobian, max_snes_failures, scale_vars) and pseudo_alpha with pseudo_alpha_minimum are named as derived. Both reports rebuilt and checked.

title: Compute noise from repeat runs in the index (C2)
description:
A test's noise is derived, never stored: rows sharing test, recipe, varied, hermes_commit, limiter, conduction_method, check_level, cores, decomposition and concurrency are repeats of one configuration, and the spread across them is the figure.

Needs a function in sdtools perftest/ that groups the index by that key and reports relative spread per metric (wall_s, ncalls, nl_its, lin_its at minimum), plus the count of samples behind each figure so a one-sample group cannot masquerade as a measurement.

title: Why is snes_fd_color_use_mat never used by PETSc? (F12)
description: options_left reported snes_fd_color_use_mat as set but never used. It appears in SNES-1, SNES-MUMPS-1 and SNES-MUMPS-2, so every run of the reference recipe has carried a setting that does nothing. Determine whether the option name is wrong or deprecated in PETSc 3.23.3, whether it is simply irrelevant when matrix_free_operator=false, or whether the intended behaviour is being lost. If it was meant to change how the Jacobian is coloured, its absence may matter for the Jacobian-reuse hypothesis in so-yjs.1.
acceptance_criteria: A statement of what the option was meant to do, why PETSc ignores it, and whether the recipes should set something else instead.
notes: 2026-09-20 audit: leftover from the 2026-08 tuning campaign archived on 2026-09-18. Eleven sibling issues were closed that day with the reason 'Archived with the 2026-08 tuning work. The new project restarts optimisation from a known recipe on a fixed build'. This one was left open by omission, not by decision. It should either be closed the same way or re-justified against the new campaign. The user decides. Note that so-yjs.2 is NOT in this group: it was updated on 2026-09-19 and its conclusion graduated into SNES-MUMPS-3, so it is live.
close_reason:
Answered 2026-09-21, from the PETSc 3.23.3 source at /home/mike/work/petsc-3.23.3.

The option is not misspelled and not deprecated. It is inapplicable to this code path, so PETSc never reads it.

-snes_fd_color_use_mat is read in exactly one place, src/snes/interface/snesj2.c line 79, inside SNESComputeJacobianDefaultColor. It sits in the `if (!color)` branch, which runs only when PETSc has to build the colouring itself from the DM or the matrix.

BOUT++ builds the colouring itself. With use_coloring = true, FDJinitialise calls updateColoring and passes the result as the context to SNESSetJacobian (snes.cxx lines 132 to 147), so `color` is non-null and the branch is skipped before the option is ever consulted. Setting it true or false cannot change anything while use_coloring is true.

Two supporting details. It is read with PetscOptionsGetBool rather than registered with PetscOptionsBool, so it never appears in -help and is always reported as left over. And it is the only knob in search-space.toml with no registration anywhere on the SNES path, which is how the inventory found it: the other 84 all resolve.

Action it implies, not yet done: the option is dead weight in SNES-1, SNES-MUMPS-1, SNES-MUMPS-2 and SNES-MUMPS-3, and it is what makes options_left non-empty on every run. Removing it from those recipes would leave a clean report, which is worth doing now that a run is refused when a varied knob shows up there.

title: Fix the SNES timestep controller settings (F10)
description:
The PID timestep controller on SNES-MUMPS-1 and -2 cannot ask for a smaller timestep. facP = (target_its/nl_its)^kP (snes.cxx:1684); both recipes set target_its=100 with max_nonlinear_iterations=10, so the ratio is always >= 10 and every successful step multiplies dt by at least 1.71, clamped only at 5.0 (snes.cxx:1691). max_timestep defaults to 1e37 (snes.cxx:221) and no recipe sets one. On failure dt is halved and the run aborts after max_snes_failures (10, or 20 in MUMPS-2). pid_consider_failures defaults false (snes.cxx:294) and no recipe enables it, so the back-off logic never runs.

Three one-line experiments, each cheap on a short test and each isolating one part in the R3 sense:
1. target_its below max_nonlinear_iterations — e.g. target 5 with max 10 — so the controller can go both ways.
2. a real max_timestep, rather than the 1e37 default.
3. pid_consider_failures = true, so growth is damped after failures.

Also worth testing timestep_control = residual_ratio, which the user reports was tried briefly without success — it deserves proper attention rather than a quick look.

Expected to matter most where the solver is stiff and dt cannot safely grow, which is where SNES has failed. Do not run these until the diagnostics work is done (R10) — without convergence reasons and iteration counts captured, a failure cannot be attributed.
acceptance_criteria: Measured effect of each of the three changes on a short test, with the controller's behaviour visible in the captured iteration counts rather than inferred.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-08-01 on test5steady, as step 1 of the CVODE-like scan. target_its 100 -> 5, against max_nonlinear_iterations = 10, everything else held:

                    wall    ncalls   nl_its  fails  jac builds
  baseline          676 s   438333    1007    731     2739
  target_its = 5    432 s   279790    1210    311     1748
                    -36%     -36%     +20%   -58%     -36%

Physics unchanged: peak target Te 131.0407 against 131.0465, 0.004%. Well clear of any plausible scatter (see so-xi1). This alone puts SNES 2.9x ahead of CVODE-2 on this test, against 1.8x before.

Note what did NOT happen, because it changes what is left to do. Nonlinear iterations went UP, not down: the run takes more accepted steps because dt now grows by 1.44 per success instead of 2.92, and the gain comes entirely from those steps succeeding rather than failing.

And the controller is still not two-way in practice. 576 of the accepted steps still converge in ONE Newton iteration, and at nl_its = 1 the factor is 5^0.233 = 1.44, still above one. So dt still only ever grows; the change made it grow gently rather than made it able to shrink. Genuinely making the controller responsive needs nl_its to rise above target, which is what tightening the tolerance would do - so steps 1 and 3 of this scan interact, exactly as the note on so-hgc warned.
2026-09-19: SNES-MUMPS-3 (new recipe in hermes-perftest) sets target_its = 7 against max_nonlinear_iterations = 10, so a step taking 8-10 iterations now shrinks dt. It also adds mat_mumps_icntl_24 = 1. It is the starting recipe for the parent runs. max_timestep and pid_consider_failures remain untested.

title: Design derived residual metrics to replace storing resid_ fields
description:
The resid_<var> fields are the only part of the core capture set with real disk cost — seven 2D fields per output step. They are not compressed at write time; they stay on during the run and get reduced at extraction, before dumps are deleted (R8). This issue designs that reduction.

Candidates, from what the residual-norm showcase notebook actually uses: per-equation share of total residual sum-of-squares (seven dimensionless numbers, comparable across time and cases); snes_global_residual (already scalar); location of the largest snes_local_residual cell as grid index or R-Z; share of the norm in named regions (core, SOL, targets), possibly time-averaged rather than per step.

Target is order ten to twenty numbers per output step instead of seven fields. Test whether that set actually supports the analyses we want — the honest check is whether a question previously answered from the full fields can still be answered from the reduction alone. SNES only; CVODE writes no equivalent (F8).

Prior art: /home/mike/work/notebooks/perftests/residual_norm_postprocessing/residual_norm_postprocessing.ipynb, including its caveats (guard cells exactly zero, no volume weighting, shares not magnitudes, end-of-step snapshots, normalised units).
acceptance_criteria: A defined metric set, plus a demonstration that it answers at least one question previously answered only from the full fields.
notes:
Scope narrowed by the user 2026-07-30: the output is scalars only. No residual field is stored outside the dump in any format, and snes_global_residual is recorded on every SNES run including under scale_vars, accepting that the weights are unrecorded (var_scaling_factors never reaches the dump; only a 'Var scaling: min -> max' log line per rescale event, snes.cxx:643-651) so it cannot be un-weighted later. What remains to design is which scalars to compute, not whether to keep fields.

Constraint on sequencing, not a blocker: widening the metric set is free while a dump exists and costs a re-run once R8 has deleted it. So dumps extracted before this issue settles should not be cleared unless the run is cheap to repeat.
close_reason:
Designed and implemented. The metric is the one the residual-norm notebook already established: per-equation sum of squared residuals over the domain, as a share of the total, no volume weighting (the solver's norm is a plain sum over state-vector entries) and shares rather than magnitudes (raw residual scales with the adaptive timestep). Seven numbers per output step in place of seven full fields.

The extractor now writes them into series.tsv as share_<equation> plus resid_ss_total, so they survive R8 deletion, and the study report has a page showing which equation holds the solver up over the run.

Sampling limit found and annotated on every panel: the resid_ fields refresh once per INTERNAL solver step, not per output. On the fast configurations resid_ss_total takes only 2 distinct values across 91 outputs, against ~70 on the slow ones — so the diagnostic's real resolution collapses exactly when the timestep grows. Anyone reading the history needs the distinct-state count beside it, which the page prints.

title: Why does the nonlinear solve fail 661 times on test5 and never on test4?
description:
RESCOPED 2026-07-31. The original question was why a near-unpreconditioned CVODE beats SNES on test5. That premise is dead: F23 re-ran both at one build against each test's own baseline and SNES-MUMPS-2 is fastest on all four short tests, test5s included. The old belief came from comparing runs across different builds and months.

The question that survives is sharper. MUMPS-2 fails 661 times on test5steady and 245 on test5stiff, and not once on either test4. Each failure rejects the step, cuts the timestep and forces a Jacobian rebuild, so 0.5 ms of test5steady takes 1131 internal steps and 2406 Jacobian builds where test4steady takes 16 and 23. At ~160 evaluations per coloured build that is essentially the entire cost. Removing the failures is the whole prize.

RULED OUT so far:
- Problem size and cost per evaluation. test5 is HALF the grid of test4 (20x100 against 40x100) and its residual evaluations are three times cheaper.
- scale_vars being absent. It is what removes the failures on test4 — across study 1 the count runs 24, 24, 23, then 0 the moment it is switched on — and test5 has it on and still fails 661 times.
- The gating equation. Momentum-gated does not mean failure-prone: test4steady MUMPS-2 is NVd+ 85% with ZERO failures, while test5steady MUMPS-2 is NVd+ 98% with 661. test4stiff MUMPS-2 is Pe 99% with zero, test4steady MUMPS-1 is Pd 74% with 24. Gating equation and failure count are independent, so 'the momentum equation is what breaks it' is not the answer.

REMAINING, in order:
1. The timestep controller (F10). On the MUMPS recipes it is structurally unable to reduce dt — target_its=100 against max_nonlinear_iterations=10 means every success multiplies dt by at least 1.71 with no ceiling, while failure only halves it. Growth outpaces recovery, so dt is driven into the failure boundary and stays there. This predicts exactly the observed pattern: a run that fails continuously without ever diverging. Cheapest test in the project, and it is already scoped as so-yjs.2 — that issue is now the direct route into this one and should be done first.
2. If the controller fix does not do it: what about test5's state makes a Newton step of that size fail where test4's does not. Only worth opening once 1 is settled, since the controller is currently choosing the step sizes being tested.

Do not re-open this as a CVODE-versus-SNES question without new evidence.

title: Abort criteria for crawling runs (R19)
description: R19's 'crawl' failure class is a run so slow it must be aborted, which needs a written trigger so aborting is mechanical rather than a judgement call each time. Candidate triggers: simulation speed (ms simulated per 24h wall, already in cmonitor row 2) falling below a set fraction of the reference recipe on the same test; projected completion time exceeding K times the reference; internal timestep collapsing below a floor. Also decide what gets recorded for an aborted run so it is still a usable data point under R19.
acceptance_criteria: A trigger a monitoring script can evaluate unattended, plus the record written on abort.
notes:
Settled for perf-bisect 2026-07-31 and implemented in run_ladder.py; generalise from here rather than re-deciding.

The trigger is a stall, not a wall-clock cap: abort when no output step has been written for 2 h. Progress is read from the dump file mtimes, not the log, because a dump advances exactly once per output step in every BOUT++ across the window while a stalling run keeps writing solver-step lines indefinitely. Confirmed on the oldest anchor: its dumps froze at 13:57 with 0 of 200 outputs while BOUT.log.0 kept growing until 16:18.

A plain wall-clock cap was rejected: it cannot tell a stalled run from a merely slow one, and would kill an old anchor that is genuinely completing. A generous 6 h total backstop is kept for a run that does produce output but far too slowly.

Recorded on abort as outcome=crawl_aborted. Extraction is attempted anyway - a partial run still yields snes_steps and steps tables showing the timestep collapse - and the case directory is kept if extraction does not validate.

title: Decide primary ranking metric: RHS evaluations vs wall clock (R15)
description: R15 records both wall-clock time and total RHS evaluations for every run, but not which one ranks recipes. Case for RHS count: machine-independent, no node-contention noise, exactly reproducible, changes only when solver settings or Hermes-3 change. Case against: it prices only one term of the cost. Settings families differ in linear-algebra work per RHS eval — a direct-LU preconditioner (MUMPS) does heavy factorisation with few RHS evals, so ranking MUMPS against a matrix-free Krylov recipe on RHS count alone flatters MUMPS. That matters because R3 makes SNES-MUMPS a reference technique. Likely resolution: wall-clock is the objective, counts (RHS evals, SNES iterations, KSP iterations, Jacobian builds, PC setups) are the noise-free explanatory decomposition, and a calibrated cost model turns counts into a predicted machine-independent time. Decide before the first wave.
acceptance_criteria: A stated ranking rule, including how recipes from different preconditioner families are compared.
notes: Largely answered 2026-07-30 by F17. Two identical MUMPS-1 runs differed 34% in wall clock (179 s slot 1, 239 s slot 3) while doing the same work to 1.8%. Loading points the wrong way — the slow one was the less loaded. So wall clock carries a large slot term that counts do not, and the rule follows: rank on work counts whenever runs span slots, and only use wall clock for comparisons pinned to a single slot. Counts are not noise-free (F16, ~2%), they are just free of the slot term. Still open: how to compare across preconditioner families, where counts price only one term of the cost (F4).
