title: perf-bisect ladder spans 10.6 months, not twelve
description:
The study describes itself as covering twelve months of development. The anchor dates say otherwise, measured from the new commits.tsv and confirmed independently: 2025-08-27 to 2026-07-17 is 324 days, about 10.6 months, across eleven distinct calendar months.

February 2026 has no anchor at all. March 2026 has two, 920ba829 on 2026-03-01 and e1fe3af7 on 2026-03-26, just 25 days apart. The ladder labels 920ba829 as February, and its own comment already flags that attribution as needing confirmation.

title: Does the all-neumann core boundary leave NVd+ near-singular on test5?
description:
The one lead the residual data itself points at, and nobody has looked at it.

Core NVd+ is 99.3 percent of the scaled SNES residual on test5steady (test4steady: 84.6 percent). test5 sets bndry_core = neumann on Nd+, Vd+, NVd+ and Pd+, where test4 uses decaylength on the SOL and PF sides and free_o3 on the core for the neutrals. Neumann on every side of the core block for a momentum variable is worth checking for a near-null-space: an undetermined core flow would show up as exactly this, and would also explain the var_scaling_factors floor at rtol being engaged.

Caveat that keeps this at P3: F24 established that which equation gates the residual does NOT predict whether the solve fails - test4steady MUMPS-2 is NVd+ 85 percent with zero failures. So a residual share alone is not evidence. What would be evidence is the conditioning of the momentum block, or a run with a pinned core boundary.
acceptance_criteria: Either a demonstrated near-null-space in the core momentum block, or a run with a non-neumann core boundary showing no change, closing the lead.

title: perf-bisect: bisection procedure for refining into a step
description:
The ladder is deliberately coarse; its output is intervals, not causes. When wall time steps between two anchors, bisect into that interval with 2-3 further builds to name the commit responsible. Because runs are cheap (tens of minutes) and builds are not, this is far cheaper than a fine comb upfront and yields an attribution rather than a sampled curve. Needs writing down as a procedure, including when a step is big enough to be worth chasing and when to stop.

Scope ruling 2026-07-31: bisecting BOUT++ itself is OUT. If a step lands on a BOUT++ submodule bump, attributing it to that bump is the answer wanted - no attempt to separate the two codebases. Keeps the procedure to one repo.

The index already carries ne_sep, te_sep, ne_target_max, te_target_max and max_dev. Report them alongside wall time and declare timings incomparable past a drift threshold, so the hazard is a visible column rather than a silent confound. title: Why did one run stall 68 s in MPI comms? (F17)
description:
Two identical MUMPS-1 runs on test4steady did the same work to 1.8% and differed 34% in wall clock. Measured: the slow one spent 80.2 s in MPI communications against its twin's 12.1 s — 33.5% of its wall against 6.8%. That 68 s is the whole difference, and it made each RHS evaluation cost 3.88 ms instead of 2.59 ms.

Two explanations are already dead. Slot placement: step2-lagjac ran in the same slot 3 with comms at a normal 5.3%. Loading: the slow run was the LEAST loaded of the six, averaging 2.02 concurrent runs against the others' 3.

Matters because it is the size of every effect we are trying to measure, and because it is invisible unless wtime_comms is checked — wall clock alone just looks like noise.

What differed: the slow run was the only one spanning 85-324 s, so it ran through the tail when the other slots emptied. Worth testing whether comms degrade when the machine empties (MPI busy-wait, frequency/C-state behaviour) rather than when it fills, which is the opposite of the usual assumption. Cheap test: the same case alone versus three-up, comparing wtime_comms rather than wall.
acceptance_criteria: Either a mechanism for the slot difference, or a measurement showing it is not reproducible.

title: Choose the two short tests, and the sequence of increasing cost (R16)
description:
R16 sets a sequence of tests of increasing cost: a short test run constantly, a second short test that is hard in a different way, then the scratch test, then that run continued to convergence. Run further along the sequence only as performance improves.

Scope narrows the choice: SNES is what we optimise (R26) and test 5 has never run on SNES, so test 5 is reference-only until the CVODE puzzle (so-yjs.1) is solved. That leaves tests 2, 3 and 4.

Proposed: test4stiff as the constant short test (4m15s, full resolution, restarted at 2ms where it is genuinely stiff, and the short form of the test R25 requires us to make fast), and test3 as the second (26s, DIII-D rather than ST40, hard because everything is changing at once rather than because it is stiff). test2stiff held in reserve as a system-size contrast for phase 3.

Caution on test 2: the hermes-perftest readme records its convergence reason as nearly always 4, which in PETSc means convergence on step size rather than on the residual reaching tolerance. If it stops because Newton steps became tiny rather than because the residual fell, its timings partly measure how fast a recipe stagnates, and a recipe that stagnates sooner would look faster. Verify once convergence reasons are captured, before test 2 is used for any optimisation.

Note: the readme's description of test5stiff is wrong (confirmed by the user) — it repeats the test5steady text. Do not trust the readme on restart points.
acceptance_criteria: Named tests for each rung, and the promotion rule for moving a candidate recipe up the ladder.
notes: Deferred 2026-07-29. This is not a one-time decision — which tests to use depends on what is being optimised at the time, so it gets made per optimisation campaign rather than fixed now. The analysis above (test4stiff and test3 proposed, test 2 suspect because its convergence reason suggests stagnation rather than convergence, test 5 out of scope until SNES works there) is kept as input for whenever the question is live. None of the imminent runs need it: the instrumentation measurements and the noise-floor work need only a cheap short test, and the CVODE puzzle needs test 5 specifically.

title: Version bump + rebaseline procedure (R18): define it and make it self-recording
description: R18 now says version bumps are deliberate — only when a needed feature lands, or when a feature's performance is itself under test — and each bump opens an epoch with its own baseline re-run. What this issue must produce: (1) the written bump procedure, repeatable step by step; (2) what gets recorded per bump — date, old and new commit, reason, baseline numbers either side; (3) where that record lives and how a result row is tied to its epoch; (4) resolve whether the expensive scratch variants (test2/4/5scratch, 45ms from scratch, 10s of hours) are inside the per-epoch baseline set or excluded — including them makes every bump cost a day or more of machine time, excluding them means version comparisons only cover the cheap, less-stiff regime.
acceptance_criteria: A procedure someone can follow without improvising, and an epoch record that makes 'which version was this measured on' answerable from the ledger alone.
notes: Ruled by the user 2026-09-19: a version bump must not invalidate a campaign; a quick rebaseline absorbs it, and a new version needs new parent runs from scratch (old seeds are not reused).
